text:
connect claude code and codex # connect claude code and codex

shield setup registers native hooks and mcp tools for a project. hooks check
supported tool requests; mcp lets the agent inspect policy and propose changes.
for your first installation, follow [the setup guide](getting-started.md).

## which part does what?

| part | what you use it for |
| --- | --- |
| native hooks | check supported requests from the agent's ordinary tools against active policy. |
| shield mcp tools | let the agent inspect policy, read guides, evaluate diagnostic requests, and prepare reviewed changes. |
| operator cli | initialize the project and confirm settings or policy changes yourself. |

after setup, restart and trust the agent so it loads both integrations.
use `shield history list` to inspect recorded requests and completion.

shield's generated mcp and hook entries use `shield` on path and `--project .`.
they contain no developer home or checkout path. shield discovers the current
project when it starts, so moving or copying a checkout requires no location
approval. reviewed policy reuse and temporary approval isolation are described in
[troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-project-was-moved-or-copied).

## install or repair an integration

run `shield mcp setup` for guided management. choose **install or repair** or
**remove owned registrations**, mark at least one integration with space on
**select agents**, then press enter. installation includes a **tool permissions**
page. review the complete changes and choose **apply reviewed changes** on
**apply mcp setup?**; **cancel** is highlighted by default. unmarked agents keep
their configuration. setup shows each integration's registration status. hub is
unavailable until this folder is a hub project, box until it is a box project,
and both on windows. during first-time
`shield init`, no marked agents means **skip for now** instead.

initialize the project with `shield init`, then run `shield mcp setup --agent claude` in an operator terminal to install native
command hooks and shield's project mcp entry. confirmation shows the owned files,
binary and project. claude uses `.claude/settings.local.json` and `.mcp.json`.
to add codex as well, run `shield mcp setup --agent codex`; codex uses
`.codex/hooks.json` and `.codex/config.toml`. no user/global settings are changed.
when the policy's rules ask for [codex prefix rules](policy-rules.md#codex-prefix-rules),
shield also writes `.codex/rules/shield.rules`. setup and every policy change
shield writes rewrite it, removing it when no such rule remains or codex is
removed. codex loads it only for a trusted project. shield never replaces a file
at that path that it did not write; status and the change's result say to move
such a file aside.
status also reports a stale file and hand edits, and `shield mcp setup`
repairs them. until then, codex asks block whatever the ask fallback, because
the file may let codex skip its sandbox. setup and policy reviews list the
prefixes a change adds or removes.

other hook groups, mcp servers, plugins, settings and codex rules files survive
installation and removal. repeating setup creates one registration per agent.
missing entries can be repaired by selecting the agent again. edited owned
entries conflict; shield preserves them and requires resolution. `shield mcp setup`
can also be driven in-session with `mcp_setup`: use `repair: true` and an
explicit claude or codex target to review reconciliation of conflicting shield
hooks and its native mcp registration. the exact changes need confirmation;
unrelated hooks and servers are preserved. `shield mcp setup`
without `--agent` resumes a confirmed interrupted plan. `shield mcp setup --remove`
removes the agents you select, and with every agent selected removes all owned
registrations while preserving policy, approvals and history.

to prepare repair from another connected project, call `mcp_setup_preview` with an
absolute enrolled `project`, explicit `agents` and `repair: true`.
call `mcp_setup` with the same selectors to request the exact host confirmation.
for example: `{"project":"/projects/acme","agents":["claude","codex"],"repair":true}`.
the review names the target project; ordinary tools remain bound to the original
connection. relative paths, unenrolled targets, removal and pending-plan actions
cannot use this target selector. when hub or box manages the selected hooks,
shield directs repair to that host with the same project and
`repair_hooks: true`: hub's `setup`, or box's `config_show` and `config_sync`,
preserving the host's publication ownership.

## set up through hub or box

in a project that uses hub or box, shield can hand its integration to that host
instead of writing each agent's files. the host then publishes shield to
whichever agents each developer chose, so nobody runs `shield mcp setup` per
agent. hub and box read the same definition format from their own folders:

```sh
# hub project (.hub/config.yml, created by hub setup)
shield mcp setup --agent hub
hub setup

# box project (.box/config.yml, created by box config init)
shield mcp setup --agent box
box config sync
```

`hub` and `box` are the first rows on the agent page. in a folder with
`.hub/config.yml` only `hub` is marked until you set something up; in a folder
with `.box/config.yml` and no hub configuration, only `box`. hub installs
alone: setup refuses `--agent hub` together with `box` or a native agent,
because both routes would publish competing shield entries. choosing one host
while shield owns the other's definition replaces it, and the review lists the
old definition as removed. setup writes two files in the host's folder, shown
here for box; hub's are `.hub/mcp/shield.yml` and `.hub/local/mcp/shield.yml`:

- `.box/mcp/shield.yml` is shared with everyone who uses the project. it names
  the bare `shield` command, so it holds no path from your machine. it tells box
  to run shield's mcp server for each agent with `--project .`, to allow the
  tools you marked on
  the tool permissions page except `policy_apply`, which always asks, and to
  install shield's hooks for claude code (`pre_tool_use`, `post_tool_use`,
  `post_tool_use_failure`) and codex (`pre_tool_use`, `permission_request`,
  `post_tool_use`), gemini and antigravity (`pre_tool_use`, `post_tool_use`).
  native tool approvals are scoped to claude and codex; google hosts retain
  native permissions and use separate shield confirmation. the hooks start
  with `{command}`, which box replaces with
  the command it launches for the server.
- `.box/local/mcp/shield.yml` is in box's private local layer. it pins the
  shield binary you ran setup with, so box launches that binary and its hooks
  call it. box accepts this layer only when it is private, so shield keeps the
  file readable by you alone and creates the folder owner-only when it is
  missing. if `shield status` reports the box integration as `changed` because
  others can read this file, run `shield mcp setup --agent box` to restrict it.

with both files the host writes the same hook entries a direct setup writes.
after confirming, run `hub setup` for hub (again after a change), or for box
`box setup` the first time and `box config sync` later, then restart and trust
the agent as below.

setup refuses `--agent hub` when the project has no `.hub/config.yml` (run
`hub setup` first) and `--agent box` when it has no `.box/config.yml` (run
`box config init` first). neither is available on windows, because the hook
commands are posix shell commands. shield adopts either file when it already
has the generated connection, hooks and permissions. yaml formatting and
known retired tool entries do not change that contract. shield preserves an
unrecognized definition for review.

`shield status` lists the host with the other integrations, and `shield doctor`
reports a file as missing or changed. `shield mcp setup --agent hub` or
`--agent box` rewrites both. `shield mcp setup --remove --agent hub` (or `box`)
deletes them only while they still hold what shield wrote; restore or delete an
edited file yourself first. removing one host never touches the other's
definition. removing them does not remove entries the host already published;
the host manages those.

moving or copying a project on the same developer account can reuse a current
private setup receipt. shield keeps the shared definition portable and can
refresh its exact owned local pin when the running binary's contents still match
the review. a fresh worktree or clone with a committed definition and no
recorded setup registers it on first use, hub's before box's. formatting changes
and entries for the retired `cache_prepare`, `policy_receipt` and `policy_repair`
tools retain that registration. omitted current tools get no automatic approval;
changed launchers, hooks, unknown tools or a foreign binary pin need review.
replacing the executable retries recognition at its next runtime startup.
the host continues to own the
agent files it publishes; copying a workspace needs no shield enrollment
callback in hub or box.

codex cannot ask at its hook, so the review shows the same
[ask fallback](#codex-approval-handling) a direct codex setup uses, allow for a
new choice. the host carries it for the codex hooks it publishes.

if claude code or codex already has a direct shield installation, installing
hub or box hands it over: shield stops managing that installation and leaves
its hooks, mcp entry, approvals and settings exactly as they are. run
`hub setup --adopt` or `box config sync --adopt` so the host takes those
identical entries over. the review lists the hand-over.

hub always hands direct installations over, and while hub is set up, setting
up claude code or codex directly refuses: run `shield mcp setup --agent hub`,
or remove hub first with `shield mcp setup --remove --agent hub`.

box hands them over by default. guided setup asks first; choose **keep direct
installations** to keep managing them. naming an agent too, as in
`shield mcp setup --agent box --agent claude`, keeps that agent's direct
installation. a kept direct installation can still be removed with
`shield mcp setup --remove`, which deletes its entries, including those box
then uses.

neither host publishes codex's prefix rules file, so shield keeps writing it
from your active policy while codex is set up through hub or box.

shield manages declared [project mcp connections](mcp-connections.md) in the
native agent files, including when hub or box supplies the hooks. hub or box
setup reviews and repairs those entries, and retains their ownership during
hand-over. removing the host definition removes these shield-owned connections
when no direct integration still covers the agent. entries the host published
remain managed by it. claude code cannot pre-approve `policy_apply` through hub
or box; use direct setup when you need that setting.

## load the hooks

restart the agent, trust the project, enable hooks, and approve the mcp
connection. in codex, review hook definitions through `/hooks`. shield cannot
override host trust or administrator restrictions.

setup's tool permissions page marks tools that can run without prompting.
all except `policy_apply` are marked by default; later setup preserves
your choices and labels them as a saved selection. to start from the current
defaults, run `shield mcp setup --reset-tool-permissions` (add `--agent hub`
or `--agent box` for a host definition). add `--dry-run` to inspect the reset without changing files. setup
still reviews the changes before confirmation.
codex uses a `prompt` server setting with `approve` for marked
tools. claude adds `mcp__shield__<tool>` entries to `permissions.allow` and
`shield` to `enabledmcpjsonservers` in `.claude/settings.local.json`.

mcp policy changes need separate approval. claude opens a confirmation form:
accept applies, while decline or cancel leaves the proposal pending. the form
works in `default`, `auto`, and `bypasspermissions` modes, independently of
ordinary tool approval. clients without form elicitation cannot apply.
codex uses its tool approval prompt; `never` approval policy refuses apply.
see [mcp review](project-mcp.md#proposals-and-operator-review).

repeating setup repairs missing tool approvals. unmarking a tool or removing
shield deletes only approvals shield added; other servers and existing approvals
are preserved. check `shield doctor --json` for missing or changed files and
binaries. status reports inspected hooks separately from retained hook activity.
hub- or box-published callbacks appear with `managed_by: hub` or
`managed_by: box` when their generated
settings match. duplicate, changed or incomplete callbacks report degradation.
`coverage.verification.agents` lists the latest retained hook event and timestamp
for each observed agent; `coverage.live_host_verification: observed` describes that history, not
an attestation of current host loading. with no available hook evidence it reports
`unverified`, which does not establish that hooks are inactive.

## intercepted requests

pretooluse checks requests against the registered project's policy.

| request | check |
| --- | --- |
| claude read | file read. |
| claude write, edit, multiedit, notebookedit | file write. |
| claude glob, grep | read of the search path. |
| claude bash and monitor commands | shell policy. |
| codex `view_image` | image-file read; calls naming another environment block. |
| codex `webrun` searches and direct url opens | web policy, as described below. |
| mcp calls matching installed packs, and managed project mcp calls | current mcp policy using configuration observations and full arguments. |

installed pack/profile policy applies automatically to matching configured servers;
see [mcp connections](mcp-connections.md). no manual association or host tool-name
approval update is needed. servers identified as having no applicable shield
policy retain host behavior. an unreadable, malformed or oversized shared
configuration file prevents that classification and blocks third-party mcp calls
when an mcp-integrating pack is active. managed calls whose project settings drift are blocked until setup is
reviewed again. codex's inner mcp calls from
code mode use the same per-call hook path.

session-management tools pass through to the host's permissions. for claude,
these include tool loading, task lists and stopping tasks, questions, plan mode,
scheduling, subagents, workflows, agent listing, skills, and mcp resource listing.
invoked tools are checked normally, except in remotely running subagents or
workflows. codex passes through plans, questions, permission requests, tool search,
timing (including the host's `clocksleep` tool), subagents, and mcp resource listing.

in every native agent integration, unmodeled internal tools defer to the agent's
own permissions. claude examples include mcp resource reads, session messages,
worktrees, lsp, artifacts and websocket watches. codex examples include
`read_mcp_resource`, plugin installation and interactive terminal input. this
also covers app tools without an mcp mapping and future internal tools.
shield returns no decision, including at a permission prompt; it does not approve
the tool or record a policy allow. named `view_image` environments and unmodeled browsing actions also defer
to codex. searches and direct http(s) opens in a mixed browsing call still receive
shield policy checks. recognized shell, file and mcp requests remain checked;
malformed requests for those mappings still block. encoded `mcp__server__tool`
calls retain connection and policy checks rather than the internal-tool fallback.
shield does not analyze commands typed through `write_stdin` into a running
interpreter, or actions requested through claude's `sendmessage`. a deny rule for
a shell command does not enforce those delegated actions.

### web requests

codex `webrun` supports `search_query` and `open` with direct http(s) urls,
including mixed batches of up to 16 modeled operations. every modeled operation
must pass. an optional `lineno` only positions the view. opaque result references,
clicks, screenshots, find and other unmodeled actions defer to codex permissions.
if a mixed call's modeled operations may proceed, shield returns no decision
for the call, including at a permission prompt; modeled refusals still apply.
the hook sees the initial url, not later redirect destinations.

### protected files and policy changes

claude can read and commit `.shield/config.yml`, `rules.yml`, and `shield.lock`,
but cannot edit them or read `.shield/state/`. reading agent settings or
`.mcp.json` asks because they may hold credentials. `.shield/.gitignore` excludes
private runtime state and cache files. to let the agent make one blocked change,
accept its [one-time request](project-review.md#allowing-one-blocked-request) in
the conversation; change configurable protection with
[`shield protection set`](project-review.md#protected-files).

agents can request command help, such as `shield protection --help`, under
ordinary command policy. help requests consist of plain lowercase words followed
by `--help` or `-h`, without other options or paths. operator actions remain
blocked through agent shell tools. agents inspect policy through mcp,
prepare proposals, and submit `policy_apply` with the returned
`apply_arguments`. you can also review proposals with `shield policy review`.
a proposal changes no permissions until accepted.

the first relevant ask supplies candidate pack/rule guidance and a proposal
route separately from the user-facing permission message. ordinary allowed
claude requests and shield mcp hook checks add no extra model context.
for project scripts, inspect definitions, lifecycle hooks, and arguments before
proposing a rule.

shell denials name up to three denied command forms and their matching rule ids
when that evidence is available. inspect those rules with `rule_list` before
proposing an allowance. a command can be denied for its argument form even when
its input file is readable; folder-access suggestions require a matching
outside-location failure.

claude ask reads and shell requests use its permission prompt or sdk callback;
without a permission host, they block. stored grants belong to the separate
[sdk consumer](claude-read-only.md) and cannot authorize native-hook retries.
arguments containing only an unresolved exit-status expansion (`$?` or `${?}`),
such as `echo "exit $?"`, keep ordinary approval instead of requiring a rewrite.
shield does not guess the status or propose exact literal arguments for it.
explicit command denials still block these requests; other unresolved expansions
retain their existing rewrite requirements.

### file reads

read-only text filters can use file-read policy when their only command match is
a yielding fallback or no rule matches. the supported `jq` forms include string
interpolation, arrays and objects (including shorthand fields such as
`{id, decision}`), slices, selections, regular-expression tests and output formats
such as `@tsv`. environment access, module loading, extra-input
helpers and file-loading options keep ordinary command review. explicit command
ask/deny rules retain precedence.
pagers such as `less` and `more` require command approval or a command rule;
permission to read their input files does not authorize their execution.

### skill folders

each native adapter automatically includes its own skill folders in the read/write
location union. agents can create, edit, list, search and read skill instructions and supporting
files without a folder proposal. codex includes `skills/` under `codex_home`
(default `~/.codex`), `~/.agents/skills`, the project's `.codex/skills` and
`.agents/skills`, and `/etc/codex/skills` on unix. claude includes `skills/` under
`claude_config_dir` (default `~/.claude`) and the project's `.claude/skills`.

skill editing follows ordinary file and command policy without settings-change
approval. claude skills can contain hooks, tool pre-approvals and shell templating;
shield does not inspect that content or mediate every host-internal execution
path. a user-library edit can affect other projects. codex's `/etc/codex/skills`
can affect other users when os permissions permit writing there. keeping skills
editable leaves this execution boundary outside shield's settings protection.

these roots open neither the enclosing configuration
folder nor another agent's user-level libraries. existing project permissions
and explicit command denials still apply. shield verifies existing ancestors
on each request, so new skill folders work without setup or a policy edit.
a symlink in the relative skill path cannot redirect this access to another folder;
links inside a library retain ordinary containment and protected-file checks.

### temporary and session files

claude and codex native adapters include the system temporary folders in the
read/write location unions. on unix this includes existing `/tmp` and `/var/tmp`
roots plus the native per-user temporary directory; macos aliases resolve to
their actual directories. existing and newly created temporary files need no
folder proposal or session ownership check. explicit command/rule denials and
protected shield files still apply. removing or replacing a temporary root
itself is blocked. this access does not edit project `access_paths`.

temporary environment overrides do not open the home directory, its ancestors
or its descendants, including `.ssh`, `.claude` and `.codex`. shield checks the
resolved directory, so a symlink alias cannot bypass that boundary. custom
scratch under home follows ordinary project access or an explicitly reviewed
`access_paths` grant.

for claude native hooks, the read union also includes the current session's
output folder, `projects/<encoded-project>/<session>/`, when the transcript path
matches the registered project, session id and configured claude directory. it
holds persisted tool results and subagent and workflow output, which the agent
can inspect through read or supported text filters. the session transcript beside
that folder, other sessions, settings, credentials and writes receive no extra
access through this session scope. directory or operand symlinks
cannot redirect this scope outside the verified session folder. the scope is
observed afresh for each callback and is unavailable to mcp diagnostic input.

claude's auto-memory folder for the registered project,
`projects/<encoded-repository>/memory` under the configured claude directory, is
readable and writable, including creating it, so claude can keep its memory
notes. as in claude, the folder belongs to the git repository holding the
project, so its subfolders and linked worktrees share it; outside a repository
it belongs to the project folder. other memory folders and the rest of the
claude directory get no extra access. a folder chosen with claude's
`automemorydirectory` setting follows ordinary policy.

for codex native hooks, installed plugins under `plugins/cache/` in
`codex_home` are readable but not writable, so codex can open its plugins'
skills. plugin staging folders, codex's memory store, which codex shares across
projects and updates itself, and the rest of the codex home get no extra access.

status lists `skills` among the supported working-file categories, `memory` for
claude and `runtime_assets` for codex. setup's review names the memory and
plugin access of the agents it configures. other runtime assets and scratch folders outside
temporary roots are not automatically discovered.

### shell analysis

bash source retains flags, quoting and compounds for conservative shell analysis.
a literal `cd` to the already known current directory, including `cd .`, keeps
that working-directory context and needs no extra approval unless an explicit
command rule asks or denies it. literal posix directory changes such as
`cd packages/ui && command` use the observed target for the successful branch.
across agents, ordinary relative targets resolve from the reported working
directory by default. a reported nonempty `cdpath` or source-level environment
change retains unresolved handling for directory search; `./` targets bypass
that search. unreported shell-local directory-search settings are outside the
shell preview contract.
`||` retains the failure directory, and `;` checks both possibilities. logical
and physical `-l`/`-p` behavior follows observed symlinks. unknown environment,
directory shortcuts and preceding unclassified filesystem changes retain
conservative handling; returning to a path after an unresolved change does not
restore known context. explanations show the cwd used for each operation.
heredocs and here-strings supply inline data without an extra approval requirement.
the command, output destinations, substitutions and shell interpreter bodies
still follow their own policy checks, so writing a quoted heredoc to an approved
project file can proceed when both the command and write are allowed.
standalone `[` and `]` in tests such as
`if [ -f agents.md ]; then cat agents.md; fi` preserve the working-directory
evidence for the read. shield checks every branch against policy; an existence
test does not authorize the read or skip checks on a missing file.
codex permitted requests return brief model context without an explicit allow
response or argument rewrite; ask fallback retains the original policy decision.
exact shell rules match the complete supplied vendor input and available context.
protected-path checks resolve existing symlink targets, including ancestors of new files.
agent shell tools cannot run shield's operator actions or launch its literal
`mcp serve` startup sequence under another executable name. help-only requests
follow ordinary policy and protected-path checks. use the registered
shield mcp tools to propose changes and request approval.
allow permits the command; deny blocks it. unmatched requests ask. when the only
explanation for an ask is source shield cannot inspect, such as `$(…)`, `eval` or
`sh -c`, the hook blocks the request and tells the agent which part to rewrite as
literal, separate commands; the rewritten request then gets its actual decision.
### codex approval handling

codex pretooluse cannot request native approval. setup preserves a saved fallback
or defaults a new choice to **allow** for every profile, including strict. the
final review shows it without a separate picker. allow includes unmatched
commands and explicit ask rules; deny, invalid requests and protection failures
still block, and so does an ask on a command a shield prefix rule covers, which
codex would run outside its sandbox without asking. repeating `shield mcp setup --agent codex`
preserves a saved block or allow choice. history retains
policy ask and the configured handoff, without recording individual approval.
automatic ask allowance is suspended while a confirmed setup plan needs repair;
run `shield mcp setup` to finish that plan.

codex also installs permissionrequest for approvals codex independently raises.
shield evaluates the request again against current policy. deny blocks; ask
returns no decision, leaving codex's approval flow in control. policy allow can
resolve the approval using the available host context. an explicit workdir takes
precedence; otherwise shield uses codex's reported session cwd for all supported
commands. missing workdir or tool ids do not change policy allow into ask.
fresh policy allow approves without a prompt or codex rules file; ask and deny
still apply. history records missing execution context as incomplete while
retaining the policy decision and its actual handoff. the reported session cwd
is the evaluation context, not proof of a hidden per-command execution directory.
with the blocking fallback, an ask stopped at pretooluse never reaches this event.
neither abstention nor completion establishes that a person approved a request.

`node --check file` and `node -c file` are syntax checks, with an optional `--`
before the single filename. this applies to bare `node`, `/bin/node` and
`/usr/bin/node`; other executable paths follow ordinary command policy.
when node has no specific rule beyond a yielding ask
fallback, shield decides the check through file-read policy. an ordinary readable
project source can therefore pass without an ask fallback or a node permission
pack. explicit command ask/deny rules, outside-folder rules and protected files
still apply. extra runtime flags, stdin and multiple filenames retain ordinary
command evaluation.
when supplied environment metadata contains node preload options in `node_options`
(`--require`/`-r`, `--import`, `--loader` or `--experimental-loader`), shell syntax
checks also retain execution review because startup code can run.

submitted relative paths use known request cwd. after a cwd change the analyzer
cannot resolve, relative file redirections and supported destructive file operations
block because shield cannot verify their targets. ordinary file moves into the
project root follow policy; replacing or moving protected configuration blocks.
redirections to `/dev/null` and between numbered descriptors, such as
`2>/dev/null` or `2>&1`, open no project file and need no policy.

finite literal `for` loops check their commands through normal policy lookup.
a supported loop and its resolved `break` or `continue` do not require approval
on their own; an explicit policy restriction still applies. for example, if
`node src/server.js` needs approval inside a loop, shield names that invocation.
unresolved command arguments or unsupported control flow can separately require
a rewrite or approval.
using `path` as the loop variable separately asks because it changes which
executables the commands select.

for a simple background command such as `node src/server.js &`, shield tracks
the runtime pid's origin through `$!`, `pid=$!`, and whole-variable copies such
as `copy="$pid"`. a supported `kill "$copy"` can therefore reach the normal
ask flow instead of requiring a rewrite for an unknown operand. known ifs must
preserve a single numeric field for unquoted targets; quoting avoids splitting.
overwrites, uncertain branch values, unsupported mutations, arithmetic, indirect
references and values read from files do not establish this provenance.
only positive pid references with supported literal signal options are modeled;
process-group and name-based targets retain ordinary evaluation.
the pid remains symbolic: shield does not know its number or verify that the
original process is still alive. this analysis never grants policy allow for
the kill; configured ask handling still applies, including codex's allow fallback.
runtime ownership enforcement requires a runner that owns the child process.

### suggestions and history

fetches that need permission return to the agent for a reusable domain review
before execution. the agent prepares `policy_apply` confirmation covering the
site and its subdomains, all paths, queries and ports. localhost service names
share one allowance. if you decline saving permission, exact one-time approval
remains available. explicit policy rules and configured automatic fallback keep
their decisions. see [web allowances](policy-rules.md#allow-searches-and-documentation-fetches).
shield remembers a save offer per domain and session. declining or cancelling
it suppresses further save offers in that session; individual requests keep
their existing permission requirements. this survives reconnecting and does
not depend on request history being enabled.

native agents can receive an initial pack suggestion when a retained catalog
advertises the analyzed command. one pack can advertise several executable names;
multiple matches are alternatives to inspect, rather than a single chosen pack.
suggestion guidance uses short names such as the `node` rule pack in conversation;
tool arguments retain the full reference. publisher and registry names distinguish
packs that share a short name.
the full registry/publisher/name reference leads to `pack_info`,
`policy_propose` and user review through `policy_apply`. a relevant
pack may still ask or deny the invocation. suggestions preserve the current
decision and change no policy; see [catalog refresh](local-registry.md#suggestions-for-commands).

with the blocking fallback, codex explains that native approval is unavailable.
the message can offer a rule for the exact command, web search or fetched host,
or an outside folder. the agent submits that change through `policy_apply`
for your approval, then retries once it is applied. cli users can also use
`shield history list` and `shield rule add` directly. `shield request approve` does
not authorize a native hook retry. policy deny requires a policy change and cannot
be overridden by ordinary host approval. web searches and fetches follow web
rules; see [policy rules](policy-rules.md). git/docker effect hints do not override
allow merely because indirect effects are possible. hooks use the submitted
command and available context; they do not verify execution.
with docker pack 0.1.0 and baseline 0.16.0 or 0.17.0, a direct `exec` or an
explicit `--entrypoint` on an allowed `--context` can read container paths
such as `/bin` using supported forms of `ls`, `cat`, `head`, `tail`,
`wc` and `find`. recognized container fetches follow web policy. for
example, `curl -q http://localhost:3200/ready` skips curl configuration
and can proceed when web policy allows the url. exact client help queries

automatic logs live in the os temporary directory under
`shield-logs/shield-<timestamp>-<pid>.jsonl`. on macos, inspect them with

server keeps a file for its process lifetime. operator commands print their log

mcp frame logging uses a separate worker with an eight-frame queue. the
dispatcher submits frames without waiting for parsing or file writes; a full
queue drops diagnostic frames. tool names are cached once per process. the
logging worker drains accepted frames with a 5 ms shutdown allowance. an unfinished
drain or dropped frames produce a diagnostic stderr warning. slow storage does
not block live ping or cancellation dispatch. frame sizes remain bounded by the
mcp input and output limits. frame records include `observed_us`, captured when
the observer receives the frame, before worker parsing or file writes.

both builds accept `--debug-log-dir directory` to enable logging into another
directory and `--no-debug-log` to disable it. `shield_debug_log_dir` also selects
the directory for child processes that inherit it; export it before starting the
agent. hosts can filter child environments. the cli directory overrides the environment, and opt-out overrides the
environment and debug default. shield uses a directory rather than a single
file because concurrent native callbacks start separate processes.

files are uniquely created, use mode 0600 on unix, and stop at 8 mib with a limit
marker. startup admission keeps shield-owned logs within 32 files and 256 mib,
reserving each live writer's full allowance and reclaiming oldest completed
logs. live writers and unrelated files are preserved; exhausted capacity disables
optional logging. a logging failure reports a warning
on stderr and disables logging without changing authorization or transport output.

records include elapsed milliseconds and pid/version/build type,
native agent/event/tool and session/turn/tool-call ids, captured input bytes,
input validity and overflow, project/snapshot preparation, evaluation, native
handoff and history stage timings, policy decision/fallback/disposition, completion
history status, response event/decision/context shape, and mcp method/tool/id,
request/response sizes and error status. commands, arguments, tool results,
policy content, project paths, credentials and raw error text are omitted. large truncated hook
input cannot supply parsed ids; its overflow and captured size are still recorded.
pair input/output records by pid and mcp messages by request id to inspect timing.
these logs are diagnostic evidence, separate from request history and execution
attestation. `rust_backtrace=1` enables panic backtraces on stderr; debug symbols
also support native debuggers.

request trace records add monotonic microsecond offsets, a wall-clock anchor,
connection/request/trace ids and fixed stage names. `request_span` durations are
inclusive of child spans; do not sum nested durations into a request total.
`request_end` reports work counters, outcome and total handler duration. counters
initialized to zero name instrumented work; absent counters have no reported
observation and must not be interpreted as zero.
`request_incomplete` means a request link was dropped without completion, not that
its mutation rolled back. fixed events and request records share a nonblocking
queue capped at 512 records of at most 32 kib each. loss appears as
`dropped_records`, `dropped_records_total`, `dropped_spans` or a diagnostic stderr
warning. operator/mcp writer shutdown waits at most 5 ms before reporting an
unfinished drain. native callbacks retain fixed hook-stage events without
creating request spans or waiting for an exit drain; recent events may be lost
at process exit. disabled logging does not construct event fields.

writes, connection publication and durable sync operations. legacy form continuations retain their request link and measure
the input or approval wait. host permission obtained before shield receives an
mcp call is outside this measurement. the handler boundary also excludes mcp
scheduler queueing, schema validation and final wire encoding; round-trip tests
measure transport overhead separately. modern form retries have separate traces.
proposal spans distinguish base capture, edits, next capture, comparison, plan
preparation, handle reservation and presentation. `policy.source_captures` counts
source validation independently of compiled-plan preparation, so re-parsing packs
cannot hide behind a zero preparation count. a process validates each exact set
of policy sources once: following the files, comparing them and rebuilding a
proposal's two sides reuse the snapshot of the same bytes, counted by

validated again.
pack spans distinguish decoding, source validation, resolution and matcher
preparation. `pattern.compiled` and `pattern.reused` count newly built and exact
reused matcher programs. rule/access-path proposal edits borrow matchers from the
preceding captured snapshot, while validating source and accounting the new

embedded enforcement handoff # embedded enforcement handoff

use `shield::enforcement::handoff` to embed shield in a trusted rust host.
it revalidates policy evidence and invokes your callback only for an allowed
operation. your host classifies requests and performs the operation.

for claude or codex setup, use [native project setup](claude-project.md).
for restricted sdk reads, use [claude sdk integration](claude-read-only.md).
the embedded api installs neither integration.

## integration contract

load a snapshot of the project's [policy files](policy-files.md), evaluate the
request, and classify it with `enforcement::agentaccess`:

| access | gate behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `ordinary` | recheck that the policy files are unchanged; invoke the callback only for allow |
| `operator` | block approval, grants, policy changes and protection disabling |
| `authorizationstatewrite` | block direct writes to the policy files, approval state or their storage parents |
| `unclassified` | block unsupported or ambiguous requests |

allow rules cannot override protected or unclassified access. ask returns
`approvalrequired`, deny returns `denied`, and state or locking failures return
`runtime` with the cause. this api cannot issue or consume approval grants.

classification is the host's responsibility; `agentaccess` cannot be deserialized
from agent json. intercept every applicable tool path, including indirect writes
to state files, directories, and ancestors. the api does not inspect paths,
resolve aliases, parse vendor tools, or verify executable identity and future
shell effects. incorrect classification defeats its protection.

## handoff and failures

the callback receives the original request/evaluation while the writer lock is
held. keep it short; do not wait for process completion or acquire another review
writer lock. changed policy files, another project's evidence or corrupt state
prevents ordinary handoff; evaluate the request again. snapshot checks do not
prove executable or filesystem stability.

the outer `result` reports protection failures; the inner value is the callback's
result. panic unwinding releases the lock. a lock-release error can occur after
the callback ran, so check its effects before retrying.

handoff consumes its evidence through rust ownership. callers can evaluate a new
request; consuming evidence is not a one-time approval grant. unrestricted
processes can still invoke the operator cli or write state.

## verified scope

local macos tests cover decisions, protected access, stale and corrupt state,
callback errors, and panic cleanup. doctests check ownership and reject json
access claims. host interception and request classification need their own
verification.

the embedded gate writes no audit history. the
[sdk adapter](claude-read-only.md) and [native runner](native-run.md) use separate
approval gates and record their own observations. none provides os isolation
from unrestricted same-user processes.

your first shield project # your first shield project

set up a project policy, connect claude code or codex, and inspect an agent
request. for an overview of the concepts, read [what is shield?](introduction.md).

## before you begin

you need the `shield` command on your path. the terminal steps below require an
interactive terminal; a connected agent uses the host's confirmation form. if you
are building from the canonic checkout, the local installer is:

```sh
cd packages/shield
cargo xtask install
```

the installer puts `shield` in `~/.local/bin`; add that directory to your `path`.
see [development](development.md) for build details. macos and amd64 windows have
native verification; arm64 windows is implemented but unverified. on windows,
follow the [portable installation instructions](development.md#portable-windows-packages)
and read the [command coverage](development.md#supported-windows-commands-and-acceptance).
on gnu/linux, use the [linux build and portable installation instructions](development.md#native-linux-development).
the linux binary's glibc requirement is recorded with its build; broader host
coverage and arm64 behavior are accepted without extra tests for this stage.

open a terminal in your project. default setup downloads a signed baseline
pack from shield's main registry, so you need network access.

## 1. initialize the project

if shield's mcp tools are already connected to your agent, ask it to set up
shield. in a fresh project it can use `init`, show you the setup review and
continue configuration on the same connection after you accept. for a combined
hub and shield setup, the agent initializes hub, registers the existing project,
configures shield through hub and publishes its hooks. reload the affected agent
to load new registrations. see [agent setup](project-mcp.md#initialize-from-an-agent-session).

from the project directory, run:

```sh
shield init
```

shield asks you to choose a profile for the **baseline**, its default pack of
permission rules. recommended is preselected. a profile selects the pack's
decisions; it does not change your agent's sandbox.

at the agent selection, use space to mark the agents to configure, then enter to
continue. agents whose commands are on your path are preselected. enter with
none marked skips agent setup; you can add it later.

review the packs, agent settings, and shield binary path, then confirm. shield
saves the active policy and creates `.shield/` for policy files and private
runtime state in `.shield/state/`. to keep the policy files in
`.config/shield/` or another file instead, see
[where the configuration lives](policy-files.md#where-the-configuration-lives).
cancel leaves the project unchanged; a failed baseline download
or verification leaves a new project unenrolled.

for a first setup with a different baseline profile, use
`shield init --profile strict`. to start without adding the default baseline,
use `shield init --no-baseline`. an empty policy returns ask for unmatched requests.

## 2. load the agent integration

if you selected an agent during initialization, its registrations are already
installed. to add one later, choose the command for your agent:

```sh
shield mcp setup --agent claude
```

```sh
shield mcp setup --agent codex
```

each command installs hooks and mcp tools for that agent after review, keeping
any other selected agent registered.

restart the agent after setup. trust the project, enable hooks, and approve the
mcp connection as the host requires. in codex, also review the hook definitions
through `/hooks`.

**codex:** new setups let valid ask requests proceed by default, even with the
strict profile. saved choices are preserved; deny and protection failures still
block. check this fallback in the review. see
[ask handling](policy-decisions.md#what-happens-after-ask).

hooks check supported tool requests. mcp lets the agent inspect policy, read
guides, and propose changes. check that both load in the restarted agent.

## 3. inspect the result

run these from the same project:

```sh
shield status
shield doctor
```

check that `status` names the right project and lists your packs and agents.
`doctor` adds diagnostic checks and recovery commands. resolve any reported
repair before continuing. both report installation state; live interception
remains `unverified`.

to inspect the rules themselves, use:

```sh
shield rule list --json
```

json output includes full identifiers and structured details.

## 4. inspect an agent request

continue your ordinary work in the restarted agent. when shield records a
request, you can inspect it in the terminal:

```sh
shield history list
```

copy an entry id from the list and use it in place of `entry`:

```sh
shield history show entry
```

find a command the agent submitted. the detail view shows its decision, matching
rules, and any reported completion. a decision alone does not show that execution
finished. if history is empty, follow
[integration troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-agent-does-not-seem-to-use-shield).

## where to go next

read [policy decisions](policy-decisions.md) to understand the result of a
request. then [find a permission pack](local-registry.md#find-and-install-a-pack)
or [write a custom rule](policy-rules.md#your-first-rule) for your project's
needs. agents can use [shield's mcp tools](project-mcp.md) to inspect policy and
prepare changes for your review.

connect gemini cli and antigravity cli # connect gemini cli and antigravity cli

gemini cli and antigravity cli use shield's shared policy engine, setup ownership,
proposal validation and session grants. native checks cover macos gemini cli
0.67.0 with a local scripted provider and logged-in antigravity cli 1.5.1.
gemini's interactive ask acceptance and cancellation are verified with the local
provider; antigravity's ordinary interactive ask acceptance and refusal are verified with the
logged-in cli. other-platform native acceptance remains separate.

from an initialized shield project, run:

```sh
shield mcp setup --agent gemini
shield mcp setup --agent agy
```

choose the agent you use, review the proposed settings, then restart it.
gemini stores hooks and mcp in `.gemini/settings.json`. antigravity uses
`.agents/hooks.json` and `.agents/mcp_config.json`. setup preserves unrelated
entries and refuses changes to owned entries that you edited manually. check
the result with `shield doctor`. remove an integration with
`shield mcp setup --remove --agent gemini` or the corresponding `agy` command.
in a hub or box project, `shield mcp setup --agent hub` or `--agent box`
writes a shared definition and private binary pin in that host's folder. with
the matching build, `hub setup --adopt` or `box config sync --adopt` can take
over existing identical google registrations. the host publishes their hooks
and mcp entries; native per-tool approvals in this definition apply to claude
and codex. google clients retain their native permissions; in-session policy
confirmation has the limitations described below.

## request coverage

both integrations check mapped shell commands, file reads and writes, searches
and mcp calls through the shared policy. unmapped internal tools retain the
agent's permission system. neither integration replaces the host sandbox.

gemini cli 0.67.0 lets a tool call continue if shield's pre-tool hook times out.
shield installs a 10-second hook limit. when that limit is exceeded, gemini
records the hook failure and continues under its native permissions without a
shield decision. a hook timeout therefore leaves shield enforcement unavailable
for that call.

relative file paths and omitted shell directories use the available workspace
context. explicit directories are honored. gemini can verify its project directory
through its native project marker; otherwise its reported cwd is the best available
context. searches and multi-file reads retain host permissions when additional
workspace roots are unknown. fetch prompts check every extracted http(s) target,
including the raw-content host for github blob links.
gemini fetch calls must supply either `prompt` or `url`, never both. mixed inputs
are refused because the host's fetch modes select different fields.

antigravity supports fresh shell commands in a single workspace and explicit
absolute `cwd`. reused terminals and ambiguous workspace defaults retain host
permissions after evaluating the modeled command; shield does not automatically
approve them based on a guessed directory. relative file paths in several open
antigravity workspaces also retain host permissions; use an absolute path for a
complete policy check. malformed mapped arguments receive recovery guidance.
antigravity's `view_file_outline` and `view_code_item` receive file-read checks.
input to an existing terminal through `send_command_input` is blocked; start a
fresh mapped command instead. gemini's legacy `save_memory` is blocked; current
memory edits use its ordinary file tools. extended gemini glob syntax such as
`@(..)` and `+(..)` is refused; use explicit directories and ordinary globs.
neither host supplies stable tool-call ids, so shield does not fabricate
before/after correlation.

gemini returns native `ask` decisions; the headless fixture waits for confirmation
without returning the requested content. antigravity uses `auto_approve` for a
fully modeled policy allow and `force_ask` for ask. its ordinary headless mode
rejects unavailable approval, but `--dangerously-skip-permissions` bypasses
`force_ask`. native deny still blocks in that mode.

these integrations support shield's mcp confirmation forms when the client can
present them. when confirmation is unavailable, the agent must close the
unapplied attempt and report the missing capability; it must not direct the user
to a terminal to accept a saved proposal. closed reviews are retained for outcome
inspection, not later approval.
gemini 0.67.0 does not advertise mcp forms. antigravity cli 1.5.1 advertises them
but cancels them without an approval ui in both interactive and headless operation,
including skip-permissions.
ordinary native ask dialogs are independent: gemini supports acceptance and
cancellation even in yolo mode, and antigravity's yes action releases the
withheld read.

gemini must trust the workspace before it loads project hooks. a successful
setup or `--skip-trust` alone does not establish that the running cli loaded them.
the native test explicitly trusts only its isolated scratch workspace.
antigravity doctor reports a disabled shield hook as a diagnostic. removing its
integration deletes an empty owned mcp configuration file and preserves unrelated
server entries and settings.

| capability | gemini cli | antigravity cli |
| --- | --- | --- |
| shared policy, setup/repair/removal, explicit mcp identity | implemented | implemented |
| native allow/ask/deny | local provider and interactive ask verified | logged-in cli and interactive ask verified; skip-permissions bypasses ask |
| policy confirmation | form adapter implemented; native 0.67.0 lacks forms | form adapter implemented; native 1.5.1 cancels forms |
| skills and current-session outputs | editable skills; read-only session outputs | editable skills; read-only session outputs |
| session grant protocol | shared implementation and transport fixtures | shared implementation and transport fixtures |
| hub- or box-managed publication | implemented; ownership fixtures | implemented; ownership fixtures |
| linux/windows native acceptance | not established | not established |

## skill folders

the integrations supply default temporary-folder access and read/write access
to their own skill libraries. gemini recognizes project and user
`.gemini/skills` and `.agents/skills`; `gemini_cli_home` selects the parent
containing the two user folders.

antigravity recognizes project `.agents/skills` and legacy `.agent/skills`,
plus `~/.gemini/config/skills`, `~/.gemini/skills` and
`~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills`. plugin libraries are not automatically
discovered. skill files can be created and edited; credential siblings and agent
settings stay protected. ordinary command and file policy still apply.
symlinked library folders cannot appoint another protected namespace.

skill editing does not require settings-change approval. shield applies ordinary
file and command policy, but does not inspect skill content for executable hooks
or permission directives. host-internal execution may occur outside intercepted
tool calls, and changes to user skill libraries can affect other projects.

gemini also receives read-only access to its current session's output directory
under `.gemini/tmp`, after matching the transcript layout, session id and
`.project_root` marker to the enrolled project. its chats directory is not granted.
antigravity receives its current conversation's brain directory only after
matching the workspace, conversation id, artifact directory and transcript layout.
sibling sessions, substituted symlinks and writes receive no automatic access.

what is shield? # what is shield?

shield checks coding-agent requests against permissions you set for a project.
you can allow a test command, ask before a deployment, or deny changes to agent
settings. its integrations check supported claude code and codex tool calls,
and its history shows which rules decided them.

## when would i use it?

use shield to share permissions across a project, add rules for your workflow,
or investigate unexpected agent permissions. agents can suggest changes, but
you review them before they take effect.

start with the default baseline pack. you can add packs and custom rules later;
the first setup needs no handwritten policy.

## how a request gets a decision

suppose an agent submits `acme-check verify`, a fictional inspection command:

1. the integration sends shield the request and available context.
2. shield checks the **active policy**: the configuration, rules, and packs you
   last confirmed.
3. shield returns **allow**, **ask**, or **deny** and explains the matching rules.
4. the agent host handles the result using its permission settings.

an allowance for that exact command does not automatically allow
`acme-check verify --write`. arguments and working directory can be part of a
rule. a request with no deciding rule returns ask.

claude can prompt for ask. a new codex setup lets valid ask requests proceed by
default, even with a strict pack profile. see
[what happens after ask](policy-decisions.md#what-happens-after-ask).

## the pieces you configure

| term | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| policy | the rules and settings used for a project. |
| permission pack | a reusable collection of rules, such as the default baseline. |
| profile | a pack's loose, recommended, or strict decision choices. |
| custom rule | a project-specific rule, such as allowing one test command. |
| registry | a source of packs. shield includes the `main` registry. |
| integration | the hooks and mcp connection registered with an agent. |

a pack contains policy data; installing it does not install the tool it describes.
profiles select pack decisions and do not configure an agent's sandbox.

## you review permission changes

shield's terminal commands show changes before asking you to confirm. agents
can prepare proposals through mcp, the interface they use to call shield's
tools and read these guides. you approve a proposal in the host or terminal.

the policy is the project's `.shield/` files. a yaml edit you make by hand
applies to the next request; see [policy files and settings](policy-files.md).

## understand the boundary

shield checks submitted requests. it cannot observe every effect of a running
command or replace your agent's sandbox. a host that skips, disables, or times
out a hook can bypass its checks.

after setup, restart and trust the agent so it loads the hooks. the
[integration guide](claude-project.md) covers supported requests and loading.
the [sdk adapter and macos runner](readme.md#integrate-with-shield) are separate
integration options.

## start with one project

follow [your first shield project](getting-started.md) to initialize policy,
connect your agent, and inspect the result. then learn
[how policy decisions work](policy-decisions.md), or go directly to
[finding a permission pack](local-registry.md#find-and-install-a-pack).

registry sources and packs # registry sources and packs

permission packs contain reusable rules for tools and workflows. registries
supply those packs; installing a pack does not install its target tool.

start with discovery below. pack authors and registry maintainers can skip to
[catalog files](#catalog-files) or [dependencies](#pack-dependencies).

## find and install a pack

from an initialized project, search the main registry and inspect a result:

```sh
shield pack search main/
```

`main/` searches the built-in registry without installing anything. copy a
result's full reference in place of `pack_reference`:

```sh
shield pack info pack_reference
```

read the description and profile decisions, then add the same reference:

```sh
shield pack add pack_reference --profile recommended
shield pack list
```

`pack add` reviews permission changes before confirmation. after acceptance,
`pack list` shows the selection and profile. omit `--profile` to choose interactively,
with recommended preselected.

profile decisions depend on the pack: installing one does not allow every
invocation, and strict does not change codex's ask fallback. see
[policy decisions](policy-decisions.md).

for github api queries, see [github graphql reads](#github-graphql-reads) for
the distinction between engine analysis and installed pack permissions.

## change an installed pack

use `shield pack list` to find an installed selection. copy its selector, using the
displayed `pack:uuid` if names are ambiguous, in place of `pack_selector`:

```sh
shield pack show pack_selector
shield pack configure pack_selector
```

`show` inspects the retained selection. `configure` walks through any variable
questions and rule overrides, then reviews the change before writing it. a
variable supplies a value the pack was written to accept; an override turns a
particular rule off or changes its decision. see
[pack variables and rule overrides](#pack-variables-and-rule-overrides) for
flags and local settings.

to choose another profile for that installed selection, use:

```sh
shield pack add pack_selector --profile strict
```

this preserves its retained version and pin and reviews the profile change.
profile changes use retained artifacts and can work offline.

to review updates for all installed direct selections, including pinned packs, run:

```sh
shield pack update
```

from an agent, the matching mcp tool is `pack_update`: `{}` selects all
direct packs and `{"reference":"gate"}` selects one. append `@version` to select
an exact release. it prepares the same
candidate and returns `apply_arguments` for `policy_apply` approval.

review version and permission changes before confirming. updated packs keep
their profiles and pin mode at the new versions. updates run only on demand;
resolution or verification failure leaves policy unchanged.

to remove a selection, use:

```sh
shield pack remove pack_selector
```

removal works offline and preserves custom rules. it refuses if a remaining
pack requires that selection; removing a root can also remove dependencies no
longer needed by another selection. inspect `shield pack list` after confirmation.
the [dependency update and removal reference](#updating-and-removing-dependency-packs)
explains these rules in detail.

## check for pack updates

`shield status` and `shield pack list` show cached availability for all direct
selections, including pinned packs. pins keep the installed version fixed until
an explicit reviewed update; they do not hide newer releases.
a newer advertised release may need a newer shield engine,
different settings or compatible dependencies; `shield pack update` prepares the
actual candidate and shows permission changes for approval.

refresh the main registry's metadata explicitly, then inspect installed packs:

```sh
shield pack search main/
shield pack list
```

replace `main` with an enrolled alias for a custom source. search downloads
catalog metadata without downloading pack artifacts or installing rules. normal
status/list requests and hooks make no update-related network requests.

metadata stays fresh for 24 hours, bounded by its signed expiration. missing or
old metadata means availability is unknown. inspection retains observation times
and distinguishes stale evidence from fresh releases. dependency-only selections
do not produce notices. an empty scope reports “no direct pack selections to check.”

interactive status/list and completed pack changes may also print a short notice
on stderr. notices are limited to once per project per day; the same installed
and advertised version pair is suppressed for seven days. json and piped
commands receive no unsolicited notice. `--json status`, `--json pack list` and
`--json pack show pack_selector` retain structured `pack_updates` inspection.

set `shield_pack_update_check=off` in the environment used to launch shield to
disable unsolicited notices; `cached` is the default. explicit inspection and
registry operations remain available. no automatic background refresh runs.

## github graphql reads

graphql analysis and permission are separate. the engine implements `graphql-v1`
for custom rules and packs that declare it. the published github 0.3.0 pack does
not use that capability: unscoped raw api calls require review, and setting its
optional `repository` boundary excludes raw api calls. updating the binary alone
does not add query permissions to the installed pack.

use `shield pack list` and `shield pack show pack_selector` to inspect the
installed version, profile, settings and rules. review available permission
changes through [the pack update workflow](#change-an-installed-pack). for
authoring custom graphql rules, see the [graphql reference](rule-reference.md#graphql-requests);
to investigate a refusal, see [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#a-read-only-github-graphql-query-is-blocked).

## register a source

use this section when you need a local catalog or a custom https registry. you
can use the pinned `main` source without replacing it with your own registration.

choose registries explicitly, then review permission packs before installing them.
project registrations are the `registries` [setting](policy-files.md#settings):
`shield registry add` writes them to your `.shield/config.local.yml`, and a
`registries` key committed in `config.yml` shares them. a project registration
overrides the same user alias. a project default takes precedence over the user
default. the reserved `main` alias pins
`https://canonic2.github.io/shield-registry/` and the release signing key in the
binary; it installs no implicit policy. the signed main catalog is published
through github pages. a network-supplied public key cannot replace the pinned root.

```sh
shield registry add acme /path/to/local-registry
shield registry add team https://registry.example.com/ --scope user
shield registry list
shield registry list --scope user
shield registry default acme
shield pack search git
shield pack info acme/git
shield pack add acme/git --profile recommended
shield pack list
shield pack show pack:uuid
shield pack update
shield pack remove pack:uuid
shield registry remove acme
```

these cli registry mutations ask for terminal confirmation. from an agent, use
`registry_add` with `{"name":"team","location":"https://registry.example.com/"}`.
using an alias already registered in that scope requests a replacement review.
compare its previous and proposed locations and trust before accepting. the
alias's default selection and installed packs stay intact; installed packs keep
their original source identity. a project registration shadows the same alias in
your user configuration. removing it reveals that user source, which the review
identifies even when the default alias stays the same.

user-scope changes publish a committed generation and retain their receipt.
after an interruption, retry the same command: shield reconciles an unfinished
approved change using its captured source. a settled add can check the presented
source again; an unchanged source reconciles its receipt, while a new key or
location requires replacement review. a successful receipt can still report
`repair_needed` or unconfirmed `durability`; that means the change committed and
needs reconciliation, not another installation. shield preserves conflicting
manual edits in `~/.shield/registries.json` and keeps the committed registrations
active. inspect both before correcting that file or preparing another global change.

shield validates the discovered catalog, then shows a human form with its
canonical location, registry identity, signing-key sha-256 fingerprint and trust
basis. https enrollment trusts the reviewed origin/key on first use; a signature
does not independently prove publisher identity. local sources show their
canonical directory and unsigned trust basis. relative directories resolve
against the selected project.

if an agent does not know the alias or location, it can omit that field from
`registry_add` to show a missing-details form. an omitted scope then requires

| `/usr/bin/false` | none |

| --- | --- |
| `hostname.exe` | none |
| `whoami.exe` | none |

runtime tests; this is not an arm64 acceptance result.

## process ownership and history

the timeout defaults to 5000 ms and accepts 1..3600000 ms, including preparation.
native filesystem calls have no hard deadline. on macos a running child gets its
own process group. sigint, sigterm and sighup are forwarded to the exact direct child and
original group; timeout sends term. a child still in that group may receive the
signal twice. after a 500 ms
grace, kill escalates even if the direct child has already exited. on ordinary
child exit, abort and guard cleanup, kill stops the direct child and remaining
original-group members, even if the direct child moved to another group. the
launcher never signals the new group it joined.
the launcher observes exit without reaping, reserves the original leader's pid
through final group cleanup, and then reaps that child. it never signals the group
after reaping. a separate 500 ms polling window requires direct-child exit and no
remaining live original-group members after kill; an observation or cleanup failure is reported as an execution
error, rather than successful completion. native inspection and reaping can block,
so these windows do not provide a hard wall-clock guarantee.
timeout exits 124; cancellation uses 128 plus the supplied signal. the direct
child's actual exit/signal remains separate from that disposition.

this covers the exact direct child and processes that remain in the original group. it does not contain
descendants that change process groups or create sessions, launch through another
host, or race group inspection with further forks. external processes joining
the group and unrestricted same-user interference are outside this ownership
contract. the supported leaf commands do not spawn descendants; wider commands
remain blocked. parent sigkill or machine failure cannot run cleanup. descendant
zombies are reaped by their parent or the os, not by shield.

on gnu/linux the same unix process owner retains the unreaped direct child's
pid and original process group. kernel procfs observations distinguish live group
members from zombies, so terminated descendants do not block cleanup merely
because the os has not reaped them. process-group/session escapes remain outside
containment, as on macos; this does not claim cgroup isolation or parent-death
cleanup after sigkill.

on windows the child starts suspended and joins an independently retained
kill-on-close job before running. normal exit, failure, timeout, cancellation and
guard teardown terminate owned job members and verify that membership becomes
empty before releasing ownership. the retained process handle reserves the direct
child's pid. ctrl-c/ctrl-break cancellation exits 130; timeout exits 124. completion
keeps the actual windows exit code and no posix signal. input/output/error console
modes are restored after cleanup. abrupt launcher loss closes the job and lets
windows terminate its remaining members. this covers job descendants; external
hosts and privileged interference remain outside ownership.

the launcher holds the project's writer lock only through verification and spawn,
then releases it before history writes and waiting. child ownership survives
post-spawn failures; errors terminate/reap the owned child. policy changes after
launch govern future requests. inherited file descriptors and shell redirection
before shield starts belong to the invoking host, not this launch boundary.

default optional history records original policy/binding, handoff disposition,
whether spawn occurred, pid and observed exit/signal/completion. cli attribution
remains caller-declared. completion links the earlier allowed decision only while
it remains retained. no stdout/stderr is captured; literal request arguments still
follow the existing redaction contract. opt-out/purge and unavailable history do
not change execution permission or child results; failures are reported separately.
the [project history guide](project-review.md) describes inspection and settings.

native acceptance covers macos 15.7.9 with x86_64 approval fixtures and amd64
windows with msvc, including exact grant retries, timeout and real ctrl-break
with console restoration. other tools, loader configurations, and platforms are
unverified. operator identity is caller-declared.

## prepare a small pack

save this complete document as `pack.yml` in your example directory:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
kind: pack
id: acme/inspect
version: 1.0.0
description: permit a reviewed inspection command
license: mit
maintainers: [acme]
engines: {shield: '^0.8'}
capabilities: [structured-rules-v1, argument-rules-v1]
rules:
  - id: verify
    decision: allow
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: acme-check
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [verify]}
  - id: publish
    decision: deny
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: acme-check
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [publish]}
```

this pack allows `acme-check verify`, denies `acme-check publish`, and returns
ask for other invocations. scalar decisions apply to all profiles. `engines`
declares shield 0.8 compatibility; use the range your own pack supports.

from the directory containing `pack.yml`, run:

```sh
shield __internal validate --pack pack.yml
```

```json
  "schema_version": 1,
  "cases": [
    {
      "name": "verify-is-allowed",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "verify"],
      "expected": "allow"
    },
    {
      "name": "extra-option-does-not-match",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "verify", "--write"],
      "expected": "ask"
    },
    {
      "name": "publish-is-denied",
      "profile": "recommended",
      "argv": ["acme-check", "publish"],
      "expected": "deny"
    }
  ]

```

run the fixture runner from the same directory:

```sh
shield __internal test-pack --pack pack.yml --cases cases.json
```

the json result should have `passed: true` and each case's `expected`, `actual`,
and `passed` values. exit status is 0 for a match, 1 for a mismatch, or 2 for
malformed input.

the second case checks that an extra option misses the exact allowance. change
its expectation to `allow` to see a failure, then restore `ask`. add allowed,
denied, and near-miss cases for your own pack.

### validate your own artifacts

`validate` accepts repeated `--pack` paths and an optional `--rules` document.
it checks each document's structure, capabilities, compatibility, and profile
ordering. it does not check the complete dependency set, cross-document
compatibility, or required variable bindings for activation.

`test-pack` evaluates each fixture under its selected profile. add
`--with-pack path` for companion packs under the same profile, up to 64 distinct
pack identities. `variables` binds the primary pack; companions use defaults.

## set the fixture context

fixtures use the production evaluator and fresh filesystem observations. cwd
and the default project root are the directory where you run the command;
additional access paths are not configured. add `--details` for matching rules,
requirement checks, branch outcomes, and guidance.

normalized shell fixtures test compound commands without enrolling a project.
they do not test native hooks, transport replies, or operator confirmation.
those checks, including extra-root behavior, need isolated enrolled projects.

### fixture fields

use `schema_version: 1` and a nonempty `cases` array with at most 1,024 entries.
each case has the following fields:

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `name` | required nonempty case name, unique in this file. |
| `profile` | required `loose`, `recommended`, or `strict`. |
| `argv` | nonempty array containing the executable followed by its arguments. use exactly one of `argv` or `input`. |
| `input` | a normalized diagnostic request, such as the shell example below. use exactly one of `argv` or `input`. |
| `expected` | required `allow`, `ask`, or `deny`. |
| `variables` | optional map binding the primary pack's variable values for this case. |

omitted variable bindings use declared defaults and are
otherwise unset. required variables without a binding or default refuse evaluator
preparation.
