understand policy decisions # understand policy decisions

shield returns allow, ask, or deny for a request. the agent host then handles
that decision using its integration and permission settings. for example,
codex can let an ask proceed, while its sandbox can still block an allow.

## packs, profiles, and custom rules

a permission pack contains reusable rules for a tool or workflow. installing
one adds policy data, not the tool itself.

each pack has a loose, recommended, or strict profile. the author declares the
decisions; stricter profiles cannot be more permissive. inspect those decisions
before choosing a profile.

custom rules express project-specific choices, such as allowing one command or
requiring an argument. they can tighten or relax pack decisions, but cannot
bypass protected administration checks.

## what the three decisions mean

| decision | meaning | what to check next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| allow | policy permits the supported request in the supplied context. | the host's sandbox and other permissions can still apply. |
| ask | policy requires review, or no rule decides the request. | the host's approval capability and configured ask handling determine the next step. |
| deny | policy rejects the request. | change the request or review an appropriate policy change; ordinary approval cannot override deny. |

invalid policy, unavailable required state, and protection failures block rather
than becoming an unmatched ask. unmodeled internal tools in native claude and
codex integrations defer to the host's permissions without a shield decision.
the separate [read-only sdk integration](claude-read-only.md) denies tools outside
its supported reads. a broader rule cannot add tool support.

## how rules combine

consider a custom rule allowing only `acme-check verify`, where `acme-check` is
a fictional tool you have reviewed:

| request | what to expect from that rule |
| --- | --- |
| `acme-check verify` | it matches and contributes allow. |
| `acme-check verify --write` | it misses because the argument list changed. |
| `acme-check publish` | it misses because the operation changed. |

a missed rule contributes no decision. if no other rule decides a supported
request, shield returns ask. to reject a form, match it with deny or an unmet
requirement that returns deny.

shield checks protected operations first, then project custom rules, then packs.

within custom rules and within each pack, more specific matches win. an exact
argument list ranks above an unconstrained command rule. ties resolve deny,
then ask, then allow; file order does not matter.

across packs, deny wins over ask, then allow. pack fallback rules yield to regular
rules from other packs. matching custom rules take precedence over packs, so a
custom allowance can override a pack denial. protected-state checks and denials
for other operations in the same request still apply.

for a compound shell request, an allowance for one command does not authorize
every other command or operation in it. see
[wrappers and shell commands](policy-rules.md#understand-wrappers-and-shell-commands)
for the analysis boundary.

## conditions and requirements

conditions decide whether a rule applies. requirements decide which result an
applicable rule contributes.

imagine a rule for a database command that requires `--read-only`. with that
option, the rule contributes allow. without it, an `on_unmet` branch can
contribute deny and explain how to correct the request. if you put the option
only in conditions, a request without it misses the rule entirely; another rule
or the unmatched ask fallback decides it.

this distinction matters when writing restrictions. start with the
[rule-writing guide](policy-rules.md), which shows both matching and requirement
examples.

## what happens after ask

claude's supported native requests use its permission prompt or connected sdk
permission callback. without a permission host, an unanswered ask blocks.

codex pretooluse cannot show a shield approval prompt. a new setup defaults its
ask fallback to allow for every profile; repeated setup preserves the saved
choice. with allow, valid unmatched requests and explicit ask rules can proceed.
the policy result remains ask, and history does not record that as individual
operator approval. codex's own sandbox and approvals still apply.

some requests still block: protection failures, invalid mapped requests, requests
requiring a rewrite, and asks fully covered by shield's codex prefix rules.
unmodeled codex internal tools retain host permissions without a shield decision.
automatic ask allowance is also suspended while a confirmed setup needs repair.
see [native interception](claude-project.md) for the exact boundaries.

the separate `shield request approve` workflow grants one exact stored request for
supported sdk reads or checked native execution. it does not authorize a native
agent-hook retry. see [action approvals](project-review.md#action-approvals).

## approving a request versus changing policy

| your intent | use | effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| let a native agent request proceed after ask | the host's permission flow, where supported | handles that request under the host's approval rules. |
| approve a stored sdk read or bounded native-run request | `shield request list`, then `shield request approve request` | grants an exact retry under that workflow's limits. |
| change how future matching requests are decided | a reviewed pack or custom-rule change | publishes a new active policy. |

a policy proposal can change future permissions beyond the command that prompted
it. review its matching scope before accepting. see
[proposal review](project-mcp.md#proposals-and-operator-review).

## inspect a decision

use `shield history list`, then `shield history show entry` with an id from the list,
to see a recorded request and the rule that decided it. use `shield rule list --json`
to inspect active rules and their owners.

an agent can use `policy_evaluate` through [project mcp](project-mcp.md#diagnostic-input-and-snapshots)
to evaluate a diagnostic request. diagnostics do not execute commands, approve
them, or establish live enforcement. native hooks evaluate the submitted command
and available context; they do not attest to every effect of execution.

for unexpected results, follow [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md#the-request-was-allowed-or-blocked-unexpectedly).

### inspect a docker environment

in a shell request, shield checks the inner program of `docker exec` and
`docker compose exec` as well as the outer docker invocation. the more
restrictive decision applies to the combined request.

use a full container id to preview the running container and its mount table.
on a unix host, start with the socket for your local docker engine. the default
socket is `/var/run/docker.sock`. pass `--socket` for a different local socket.

```sh
shield docker inspect container_id --path /work/config.yml
shield --project . --json docker inspect container_id --path /work/config.yml
```

repeat `--path` to look up several absolute container paths. an explicit
`--project` adds the project's read and write policy decisions for each candidate
host path. the preview uses the deepest reported mount and reports its write
mode separately from host policy. the path mapping is lexical. container symlinks and
submounts can affect what a process actually opens. inspection is read-only and
supplies diagnostic evidence for review.

policy files and settings # policy files and settings

shield enforces exactly what your project's policy files say. there is no
saved copy to activate or repair: the next request after a file changes is
decided by the changed file.

## the files

the policy files live together in one folder, the authoring bundle: `.shield/`
by default. the table uses that location.

| file | committed | holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `.shield/config.yml` | yes | selected packs and profiles, pack settings, connections, shared settings |
| `.shield/rules.yml` | yes | your project's custom rules |
| `.shield/shield.lock` | yes | the exact pack releases the configuration selects |
| `.shield/config.local.yml` | no | your own settings and pack values, layered over `config.yml` |
| `.shield/rules.local.yml` | no | your own custom rules |
| `.shield/shield.local.lock` | no | releases your local layer selects |
| `.shield/.gitignore` | yes | keeps the local files and `state/` out of git |
| `.shield/state/` | no | runtime state: pending requests, grants, history and proposals |

`shield init` writes these files. a copied, moved or cloned folder needs no
follow-up command: its files are its policy, and a folder without runtime state
gets it on first use.

## where the configuration lives

shield uses the first of these that applies:

1. the file you pass with `--config path`.
2. `.shield/config.yml`.
3. `.config/shield/config.yml`, for projects that group tool settings under
   `.config/`.

the two default folders are never combined. when `.shield/config.yml` exists,
shield uses it even if it is invalid, and reports the problem rather than
falling back to `.config/shield/`. a `--config` file that is missing or
unreadable is refused; shield does not use a default instead.

the rules, locks and local files sit beside the selected `config.yml`, and
paths inside the configuration are relative to that folder. with the grouped
layout the bundle is `.config/shield/`, which gets its own `.gitignore` for the
local files:

```text
.config/shield/
  config.yml
  rules.yml
  shield.lock
  config.local.yml   # not committed
  .gitignore
.shield/
  .gitignore
  state/             # runtime state, always here
```

runtime state stays in `.shield/state/` whichever configuration is selected.
`shield status` shows the selected file and any default file it is not using:

```text
configuration: .config/shield/config.yml
```

`--config` works with every command, including `shield init`, which creates
the file there. a relative path is resolved from the folder you run the command
in. without `--project`, the project is the nearest folder above you that
holds the `--config` file or shield's own files, so a checkout whose only
configuration is that file works from its root or any subfolder. when you set agents up with `--config`, shield adds the same file, relative
to the project, to the hooks and mcp entries it writes, so agents enforce the
same policy. that file must be inside the project. the box integration uses a
default location; use `.config/shield/` there instead of `--config`.

folders that earlier releases set up keep their state in `.shield/review/`;
shield renames it to `.shield/state/` the first time it opens the folder, and
adds `state/` to `.shield/.gitignore`.

## change the policy

change policy with the commands, which show the change, ask you to confirm it
once in the terminal and write the files:

```sh
shield pack add acme/node
shield rule add
shield policy review
```

`shield policy review` also reviews an agent's pending proposal. an agent cannot
confirm its own change: commands that change policy refuse `--json` and
non-interactive use, and native hooks block agents from writing `.shield/`.

you can also edit the files by hand. shield reads them on the next request; an
edit that makes them invalid prevents policy from authorizing requests, and
`shield status` names the problem. supported native requests can still use an
exact one-time review through `request_approve`; fixed protected paths stay
closed. for git conflict recovery, see
[allowing one blocked request](project-review.md#allowing-one-blocked-request).
a command writes on top of your edit rather
than discarding it. if the files change between showing a change and your
confirmation, shield refuses and asks you to run the command again.

pack artifacts are fetched by digest from `shield.lock`. when a release is
missing on this machine, `shield status` fetches it.

## settings

settings are keys in `config.yml` or `config.local.yml`. a key set in the local
file wins over the shared one, setting by setting, except `registries`, which
the local file replaces whole. commands that change a setting write it to
`config.local.yml`; commit a value in `config.yml` to share it.

```yaml
# .shield/config.local.yml
enforcement: enabled
protection:
  agent_settings_read: ask
  agent_settings_change: block
ask_fallback:
  codex: block
history:
  enabled: true
  limit: 5000
```

| key | values | default | changed by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `enforcement` | `enabled`, `paused` | `enabled` | `shield enable`, `shield disable` |
| `protection.agent_settings_read` | `ask`, `allow` | `ask` | `shield protection` |
| `protection.agent_settings_change` | `block`, `allow` | `block` | `shield protection` |
| `ask_fallback.<agent>` | `block`, `allow`: what a host that cannot ask does with a request policy asks about | `block` | `shield mcp setup` |
| `history.enabled` | `true`, `false` | `true` | `shield policy review` |
| `history.limit` | 1 to 10000 entries | 5000 | `shield policy review` |
| `registries` | `sources` by alias and an optional `default` alias | none | `shield registry add`, `remove` and `default` |

settings do not change what a rule decides. an invalid setting does not pause
shield: native requests ask until it is fixed.

## compiled plans

shield compiles the files into a plan stored in your cache folder and reuses it
until a file changes. deleting the cache changes nothing; the next request
compiles again. see [compiled policy cache](compiled-cache.md).

## updating shield

shield converts older saved state the first time a command, mcp connection or
hook opens the project, writes any settings an earlier version held into
`config.local.yml`, and keeps a private recovery copy. existing approvals keep
their scope, expiry and single use. `shield status` reports the conversion for
seven days.

for recovery by symptom, use [troubleshooting](troubleshooting.md).

## your first rule

suppose you have reviewed a tool's `verify` operation and want to allow it.
we use the fictional executable `acme-check`; substitute your own reviewed tool.

in an initialized project, run `shield rule add` and choose **exact command
arguments** (`argv`). enter id `verify-project`, executable `acme-check`,
arguments `["verify"]`, and decision allow. the arguments array excludes the
executable. review and confirm to write the rule for the project cwd.

the default **complete request** form also binds vendor context and environment.
choose the argument form here so the rule can cover more than one exact request.

for yaml, use this complete document. its cwd condition also covers project
subdirectories:

```yaml
schema_version: 1
kind: custom
capabilities: [structured-rules-v1, argument-rules-v1, location-v1]
rules:
  - id: verify-project
    decision: allow
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: acme-check
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [verify]}
      cwd: {within: {root: project}}
```

merge the rule and capabilities into the file selected by `.shield/config.yml`.
for a new shared file, save it as `.shield/rules.yml` and set `rules: rules.yml`
in the existing configuration. the next request follows the saved file; run
`shield status` to check that the files are valid.

`domain: argv` matches an executable and argument list. here, the executable
must be `acme-check`, the arguments exactly `[verify]`, and cwd inside the project.
`capabilities` declares the syntax used: structured rules, arguments, and locations.

| submitted command | does this rule match? |
| --- | --- |
| `acme-check verify` inside the project | yes; the rule contributes allow. |
| `acme-check verify --write` | no; the argument list differs. |
| `acme-check report` | no; the operation differs. |
| `acme-check verify` outside the project | no; the cwd condition fails. |

a miss leaves the decision to other rules, or ask if none matches. protected-file
checks and other operations in the same shell request still apply. inspect the
active rule with `shield rule list --json`, or preview a request through
[mcp diagnostics](project-mcp.md#diagnostic-input-and-snapshots) without executing it.

imported rules can carry `historical_matcher` or `historical_normalized` fields
that preserve their original matching behavior. leave such a rule unchanged
when editing other rules. to replace it, write the complete intended scope using
current `conditions` and remove the historical annotation; reviews reject new
or modified annotations and copies into another configuration layer.

## choose the right matching style

use `exact` when only one complete argument list should match. use `options`
when you have reviewed optional flags or value-taking options. use `prefix`
only when every remaining argument may be unrestricted. for example, allowing
the prefix `verify` also allows `verify --write`; it does not infer which flags
are read-only.

for example, if you have also reviewed `acme-check verify --verbose`, replace
only the first rule's `arguments` value with this fragment:

```yaml
arguments:
  kind: options
  prefix: [verify]
  flags: [--verbose]
  values: []
  operands: false
```

now both `acme-check verify` and `acme-check verify --verbose` match. the flag
is optional. `acme-check verify --write` and `acme-check verify report.txt`
still miss because the grammar declares neither that flag nor operands. keep
the executable and cwd conditions, then save the edit as before.

unless marked complete, examples below are fragments for the `rules` array.
add their [required capabilities](rule-reference.md#capabilities) to the document.

## match commands and enforce requirements

suppose the fictional `acme-db` tool must use `--read-only`. matching that flag
in conditions would leave invocations without it to other rules. put it in
requirements to decide what happens when it is missing.

merge this complete example into your configured rule file, as in
[your first rule](#your-first-rule):

```yaml
schema_version: 1
kind: custom
capabilities:
  - structured-rules-v1
  - argument-rules-v1
  - requirements-v1
rules:
  - id: database-readonly
    decision: allow
    conditions: {domain: argv, executable: acme-db}
    requirements:
      arguments:
        kind: options
        prefix: []
        flags: [--read-only]
        values: [--user]
        operands: false
        require_all: [--read-only]
    on_unmet:
      decision: deny
      message: add --read-only and submit a revised request.
      alternatives: [acme-db --read-only]
```

conditions match every `acme-db` invocation. requirements demand `--read-only`,
accept an optional `--user` value, and reject operands. failure returns the
`on_unmet` decision, deny:

| request | this rule's result | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `acme-db --read-only` | allow | the required flag is present. |
| `acme-db --read-only --user analyst` | allow | the optional value-taking option is declared. |
| `acme-db --user analyst` | deny | the required flag is absent. |
| `acme-db --read-only --write` | deny | the requirement does not accept `--write`. |
| `another-db --read-only` | no match | the executable condition does not match. |

other matching rules and protected-state checks still affect the
[final decision](policy-decisions.md#how-rules-combine). verify the real tool's
behavior before treating an option as read-only.

### require a particular option value

a valued option can also require a specific value. this rule allows
`aws logs filter-log-events` with the `acme-read-only` profile and denies the
same operation with any other profile or none:

```yaml
  - id: logs-read-only-profile
    decision: allow
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: aws
      arguments:
        kind: options
        leading: {flags: [], values: [--profile, --region]}
        prefix: [logs, filter-log-events]
        flags: []
        values: [--profile, --region, --log-group-name, --filter-pattern,
                 --start-time, --end-time, --limit, --output, --query]
        operands: false
    requirements:
      arguments:
        kind: options
        leading:
          flags: []
          values: [{name: --profile, match: acme-read-only}, --region]
        prefix: [logs, filter-log-events]
        flags: []
        values: [{name: --profile, match: acme-read-only}, --region,
                 --log-group-name, --filter-pattern, --start-time, --end-time,
                 --limit, --output, --query]
        operands: false
        require_all: [--profile]
    on_unmet:
      decision: deny
      message: use --profile acme-read-only for log filtering.
```

the conditions declare the operation's grammar without a profile value, so
every request using those options reaches the rule, whether `--profile` comes
before or after the operation. the requirements repeat the grammar and add the
value: the match applies to every `--profile` occurrence in both phases, and
`require_all` counts both phases together. another profile, a missing profile
or a second, different `--profile` gets the deny. a request with an option the
grammar does not declare does not match the rule; other rules decide it.
a pack can replace the literal profile with `{var: profile}` so each project
chooses its own, as described in pack variables below.

### conditions versus requirements

conditions determine whether a rule applies. requirements determine its successful
or unmet outcome. `on_unmet.decision` is ask or deny, and may carry a short message
and up to three static alternatives. alternatives are candidates that must be
evaluated again. they cannot rewrite requests, approve execution or bypass another
rule. put exclusions in requirements when failure should block with an explanation.
for an unmet requirement, feedback offers an `access_path_add` alternative only
when the same rule and operation report an outside-location failure. unknown
target evidence, excluded paths and unsupported options do not establish that
adding a folder would help.

## match text and arguments

use a **text selector** to match one field, such as an executable name or one
argument. use an **argument selector** to describe the whole list after the
executable. for `acme-check verify --verbose`, the executable is `acme-check`
and the argument list is `["verify", "--verbose"]`.

text selectors accept a literal string or one of `exact`, `prefix`, `one_of`,
`glob` or `regex`. regex matches the entire field, including alternatives and
inline flags. glob matches individual fields; `*` does not cross a path separator,
and an argv glob never expands into more arguments. each argument stays separate.
use recursive stars as `**/name`, `dir/**`, `dir/**/name`, or bare `**` for the
whole field. other adjacent-star placements, including `a**b`, `***` and bare
`**` inside a brace alternative, are refused. use `[*][*]` for two literal stars.
brace alternatives may contain character classes, such as `{[ab],c}`; empty
or nested alternatives are refused.
argument kinds are `any`, `exact`, `prefix`, `sequence`, `options` and restrictive
`risk_tokens`. options declare arity, leading global options, value predicates,
presence/forbidden checks, repetition and parsing settings explicitly.
with `prefix-leading-v1`, a `prefix` selector can also declare `leading` options.
it consumes those options and their values, matches the operation immediately
after them, and leaves the suffix unconstrained. this lets an administration
restriction cover unknown suffix options without matching words in option values
or later operands.

many clis accept their global options after a subcommand too, such as clap
options declared `global = true`. set `interleaved: true` in `leading`, with
`interleaved-leading-v1`, to also accept the declared leading options between
prefix words. this rule then denies both `acme-vcs --json branch remove old` and
`acme-vcs branch --json remove old`:

```yaml
id: no-branch-removal
decision: deny
conditions:
  domain: argv
  executable: acme-vcs
  arguments:
    kind: prefix
    values: [branch, remove]
    leading: {flags: [--json], values: [--project], interleaved: true}
```

only declared leading options are skipped between words. an undeclared option
or `--` there makes the rule miss: `acme-vcs branch --verbose remove` is decided
by your other rules. use this setting only when the tool accepts every declared
leading option, with the same meaning, at each level of the prefix; `git -c`
means something else after `git commit`.

for reusable allowances, choose a grammar for the operation rather than copying
one observed argv. `exact` matches only the complete literal argument vector.
`prefix` leaves every later argument unrestricted, so it is unsuitable when only
reviewed optional flags should be allowed. `sequence` fixes initial token
selectors in `prefix` and declares a `rest`: `{kind: none}`, `{kind: any}` or
`{kind: each, match: selector, min: n, max: n}`. counts default to 0–256.

an `options` grammar fixes the initial operation in `prefix`, declares boolean
options in `flags`, value-taking options in `values`, and positional arguments in
`operands`. declared options are optional unless required explicitly; unknown
options fail matching. `operands: false` rejects positional arguments;
`operands: true` accepts them without restriction. a bounded operand object
declares `match`, `min` and `max`. the `--` separator ends option parsing, so flags
forwarded through it must be modeled as operands.

an options grammar can set `unknown_options: skip` with `unknown-options-v1`
to inspect declared options while leaving unrelated options unmodeled. following
tokens remain operands or declared options; skipping does not hide them.
with `short_clusters: false`, only the first letter of a single-dash token is
checked as a short option. this prevents go-style names such as
`-future-display` from being mistaken for a cluster containing a declared `-r`.
with clustering enabled, any declared letter in a cluster still forces parsing
so an unknown leading letter cannot hide a checked option. skipping does not
establish the effects of the options passed over.

### example: permit a project test script and its watch option

suppose your project's `package.json` defines `test`, and you have reviewed both
the script and its `--watch` behavior. inspect any `pretest` and `posttest`
scripts too, because npm can run them as part of the command. use this rule
fragment to cover the base command and that optional forwarded argument:

```yaml
id: npm-test
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: argv
  executable: npm
  cwd: {within: {root: project}}
  arguments:
    kind: options
    prefix: [test]
    flags: []
    values: []
    operands:
      match: {exact: --watch}
      min: 0
      max: 1
```

this covers `npm test` and `npm test -- --watch`, including the empty forwarding
form `npm test --`. other scripts, flags, extra operands and repeated watch
arguments do not match. review script definitions, lifecycle hooks and argument
effects before proposing; an allowance permits future edits to the script too.
read [rule suggestions](project-mcp.md#rule-suggestions) for the mcp workflow.

## restrict paths

use path predicates when the same command should be treated differently depending
on the files it affects. a command's working directory and its target files are
different checks: running inside a project does not prove that every operand is
inside it.

choose the check according to what you need to establish:

| check | question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `cwd` | where does this command start? |
| `targets` | are the affected paths that shield can model inside an allowed location? |
| `argument_paths` | do the explicit path arguments satisfy the declared restrictions? |

for example, a command started inside the project can still name
`/path/to/another-project/file.txt`. a cwd check alone does not constrain that
operand. path checks depend on the supported operation model described below;
they do not turn an arbitrary executable into sandboxed code.

locations use `exact`, `within` or `outside` path predicates with `project`,
`absolute`, `read` or `write` roots. the latter two bind the approved root unions
from [project configuration](project-review.md#additional-access-paths) and require
`access-paths-v1`. `outside` means outside the entire union; an exclusion applies
under every referenced root. `within` can include a root-relative text match.

for a command limited to the project root, use
`cwd: {exact: {root: project}}`. to include subdirectories, use
`cwd: {within: {root: project}}`. the value of `exact` is a path-reference object,
not a path string. project rules use the portable `project` root rather than a
machine's absolute checkout path; changing `exact` to `within` broadens the rule.

an allow must cover all affected resource actions. fixed native rm/rmdir/cp/mv
forms and typed file operations account for source and effective destination
paths. bounded native `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `wc` and nonrecursive `ls` forms model
read operands; unsupported options and helpers retain incomplete coverage. bare
`ls` reads cwd; `-` is stdin for the other four commands. unknown options,
unresolved paths and recursive copies cannot establish
positive containment. observations are fresh per request. fixed operations use
direct path facts; bounded search metadata checks are described below.
linux/windows native acceptance is not established by macos tests.

### check paths in command arguments

`argument_paths` checks paths explicitly supplied to a tool without claiming a
complete resource model for everything that tool executes. it requires
`argument-paths-v1`, `argument-rules-v1` and `location-v1`; read/write root unions
also require `access-paths-v1`. for example, in a rule's requirements:

```yaml
argument_paths:
  grammar:
    kind: options
    prefix: [build]
    flags: [--locked]
    values: [--manifest-path, --target-dir]
    operands: false
  options:
    --manifest-path:
      path: {within: {root: read}}
    --target-dir:
      path:
        within: {root: write}
        exclude: [{root: project, path: .shield}]
      recursive: true
```

the grammar must parse the complete invocation. every occurrence of each selected
option is checked with physical symlink/ancestor resolution; unknown syntax or
unresolved context fails the requirement. `operands: {path: ...}` beside `options`
checks positional operands. absent options introduce no paths; use `require_all`
in the grammar when one must be supplied. these checks do not constrain implicit
configuration, build scripts, imports or runtime file access. the rule still
needs its own execution decision and `on_unmet` branch.

### search files with grep and ripgrep

shield models a bounded set of gnu and bsd `grep` options. options that only
shape matching or output, such as `-a1`, `-o`, `-m 3` or `--color=always`, need
no listing. the checked paths are the files grep reads: explicit regular files,
or with `-r`/`--recursive`, regular files and directories, plus `-f` pattern
files and `--exclude-from` files. a pattern given with `-e` or `-f` makes every
operand a path. a grep that names no file, such as `git show head:yarn.lock |
grep -n -a1 pattern`, reads only its input and meets a read requirement. a
recursive search reads every existing entry below each directory, hidden ones
included, and follows no descendant links; without a path it checks the working
directory. `--include`, `--exclude` and `--exclude-dir` are accepted but do not
narrow the checked footprint. options may follow the operands, written as one
word such as `--include=*.prisma`. `-r`, bsd `-s`/`-o`, a bare `-c` or `--context`
(write `-c3` or `--context=3`), ambiguous abbreviations and options outside the
modeled set remain unverified. `-d`/`--directories` accepts exact lowercase
`read`, `skip` or `recurse`; other values remain unverified. fixed `rg` forms search a pattern in explicit files or
directories, the working directory when none is given, or list them with `--files`.
options are read the way ripgrep reads them, anywhere before `--`, so
`rg -n pattern src -g '*.ts'` checks `src`. options that only shape matching or
output, such as `--sort`, `-o`, `--json` or `-e pattern`, need no listing.
`-f` pattern files and `--ignore-file` files are checked like explicit files.
walks follow no descendant links; explicit operands still follow links and receive
containment/exclusion checks. content searches can honor ignore files and glob
filters or search hidden files with `--hidden`. their footprint conservatively
includes existing hidden descendants; declared policy exclusions still apply.
native callbacks check explicitly named protected paths and auxiliary files,
without scanning search descendants or imposing directory-size or depth limits.
a search of an approved folder follows policy even when protected files exist
below it. direct reads of shield state or caches remain blocked, and direct
agent-settings reads retain their approval requirements.
`--no-ignore` without glob filters supplies a visible-only footprint.
a `--files` listing supports `--hidden` and globs and skips the native
content check; declared policy exclusions still apply. hidden listings retain
the existing-entry footprint even with `--no-ignore`. a `-` operand, helper programs (`--pre`,
`--pre-glob`, `-z`, `--hostname-bin`), `-l`/`--follow`, informational modes such
as `--version` and options ripgrep does not define remain unverified. `--no-config` is optional. shield trusts ambient ripgrep configuration
and evaluates the submitted arguments; flags injected by `ripgrep_config_path`
are outside these checks. use `--no-config` when config-free execution is desired.

### write git diff output

shield checks explicit output files as write targets for `git diff`,
`git show`, `git log`, `git diff-tree`, `git diff-index` and `git whatchanged`.
for example, `git diff head --output=review.diff` can satisfy
`targets: {action: write, all: {within: {root: write}}}` when the output
resolves inside a writable root. relative destinations use git's working
directory, including changes from `-c` that the policy normalizes. the model
accepts one leading `--no-pager` or `-p`, then one no-op editor setting
(`-c core.editor=true`, `-c core.editor=:`, `-c sequence.editor=true` or
`-c sequence.editor=:`), and leaves other global options unverified.

shield checks every `--output=file` and `--output file` before `--`.
recognized options such as `--line-prefix` consume their values first.
unknown option syntax, missing or empty output values, apparent output options
after `--`, and earlier shell operations that may change the filesystem leave
the write footprint unverified. a direct file comparison can read outside the
repository even without `--no-index`. when `git diff` can compare files directly,
a writable output alone supplies insufficient coverage.
commands without `--output` supply no write evidence. in a pack, use a
precondition that matches the output option so git commands that print
to standard output continue through the pack's ordinary rules.

### read and transform file content

fixed `sed`, `awk`, `jq`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `diff` and `cmp` forms model
explicit regular-file inputs, including contained symlink targets. read-only
forms accept missing inputs too: shield checks their paths and lets the
tool return its normal file-not-found error. outside or excluded paths,
dangling symlinks and other unverifiable inputs remain restricted. sed supports
scripts of `p`, `d`, `s`, `y`, `w`, `w`, `r` and `r` commands separated by `;` or
newlines, each with an optional numeric, `$` or slash-delimited regex address
or range, including mixed ranges, escaped slashes, `i`/`m` regex flags and `!`
inversion. for example, `sed -n '/start/,/end/p' file` reads only file.
`s` accepts the
`g`, `p`, number, `i`/`i`, `m`/`m` and `w` flags. files a script writes (`w`,
`w`, the `w` flag) are write targets and files it reads (`r`, `r`) are read
targets; a file name runs to the end of its line. in-place editing (`-i`,
`-isuffix`, `--in-place[=suffix]`) makes each input a write target too, plus
its backup when a suffix is given; when either name is a symbolic link, the
write target is the link itself, which sed replaces. because gnu sed reads
`-i word` as a script and bsd sed reads word as a backup suffix followed by the
script, such a form counts the targets of both readings and is modeled only
when both are. this includes `-i ''`: gnu sed reads the empty word as an empty
script and the following script word as another file to edit, so
`sed -i '' 's/a/b/' notes.txt` is also read as editing a file named `s/a/b/`.
when the whole command is that one sed invocation, with literal words and no
redirections or variable assignments, it is checked through an agent hook, and
it keeps no backup and writes no `w` file, sed creates nothing it could then
edit, so a named input that does not exist adds no target. a backup or `w` file could create a later
input, and so could anything else the command runs, so in those cases a missing
input leaves the edit unmodeled. `-isuffix` means the same to both. rules decide these targets like any
other read or write, so an allow limited to project reads does not cover an
edit. the `e` command and flag, blocks and gnu's `*` backup
suffixes remain unmodeled; awk supports print statements of
numeric fields, optionally with `-f`; jq supports expressions that compute only
from their input, such as field lookups, `select`, `map`, `sort_by`, `@tsv` and
variables from `as` or `--arg`, but not `$env`, `env`, `input`, modules or
program files (`-f`, `--slurpfile`, `--rawfile`). their submitted
syntax does not load program files, run helpers or access the environment, and
loads no input other than the named targets.
sort output files, uniq's second output operand and arbitrary programs
remain unmodeled. options precede the program and file operands. a `-` operand
reads standard input. packs decide whether to allow these forms or ask.

### base64 transformations

base64 encoding and decoding model file operands and input options as reads,
and output options as writes. standard input/output and `-` name no file.
a rule can check both read and write targets: a complete stream transformation
proves when either collection is empty. gnu `-i` ignores garbage; macos `-i`
names an input file. the model handles decoding, wrapping, attached values,
short clusters, repeated file options and `--`; unknown options and malformed
arguments remain unverified. every file still needs its usual path permission,
including resolved symbolic links. windows base64 semantics are unmodeled.

for example, baseline coverage can allow `command | base64 -d | grep pattern`.
the producer and every downstream command keep their own policy decisions;
decoding grants no permission to execute the decoded data.

### create directories and files

fixed `mkdir`/`touch` forms model writes;
`mkdir -p` supports new paths but operands containing `..` remain unverified.
touch reference/date options and its special `-` operand remain unverified.
for these four models, options precede operands; a leading `--` admits literal
option-like operands. these models supply resource facts; pack rules choose
permissions and supported option subsets.

## understand wrappers and shell commands

allowing a command does not automatically allow every wrapper around it. shield
looks through supported wrappers to evaluate the inner command, but the wrapper
can still require review because it changes how that command runs.

launch wrappers and child shells are looked through. `env`, `nice`, `nohup`,
`timeout`, `command`, `builtin`, `exec` and `sudo` with recognized options are
unwrapped, and rules decide the command they launch. an inline script run by
`sh`, `bash`, `dash` or `zsh`, by bare name or from `/bin`, with `-c` is read as
shell source and each command in it is decided. a deny inside the script blocks
the whole request: with a rule that denies `sudo`,
`nohup zsh -lc 'make docs; sudo true'` is denied. the wrapper or
child shell itself still asks, because it changes how the command runs, so a
wrapped request never reaches allow.

unknown options leave a child shell's script unread, and an unread script asks.
zsh accepts only `-c`, `-e`, `-u`, `-v`, `-x`, `-l` and `-f`. its script is read
with posix rules only when it contains none of the syntax that zsh handles
differently: `$`, backticks, `*`, `?`, `[`, `]`, `{`, `}`, `(`, `)`, `~`, `^`,
`#`, `!`, `%`, a word starting with `=`, `&>`, `|&`, `&|`, `<<<`, or `>&` and
`<&` followed by anything but a descriptor number or `-`. these characters
count even inside quotes.

rules also cover `shell`, `file`, `web`, `mcp` and completely bound
`exact_request` inputs. file rules permit sdk reads, for example:

```yaml
id: notes
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: file
  action: read
  sources:
    all: {exact: {root: project, path: notes.txt}}
```

this rule needs `location-v1` and `structured-rules-v1`. see the
[capability reference](rule-reference.md#capabilities) for other features.
pack documents also declare identity and release metadata. their decisions can
be scalar or complete monotonic loose/recommended/strict maps; custom decisions
are scalar.
a pack rule can set `fallback: true` so it applies only when no other pack
decides the request, such as a broad review rule a tool-specific pack replaces.

## allow searches and documentation fetches

use web rules to describe the searches or hosts an agent may access. a fetch
allowance can name one documentation host without allowing every url.

web rules decide claude's websearch and webfetch and codex's searches and
direct http(s) url opens. an open is a typed fetch with method get. each search
or open in a supported codex batch is evaluated; deny blocks the whole call,
and ask follows the configured host approval behavior. unsupported forms block
before policy evaluation. initial-url permission does not cover unobserved redirects.
this pair allows any search and fetches from one documentation host, and needs
`regex-v1` and `requirements-v1`:

```yaml
- id: search
  decision: allow
  conditions: {domain: web, action: search, query: {regex: "(?s).*"}}
- id: docs
  decision: allow
  conditions: {domain: web, action: fetch}
  requirements:
    url: {schemes: [https], hosts: [docs.example.com]}
  on_unmet: {decision: ask}
```

hosts match exactly by default. set `subdomains: true` in the url predicate to
include a domain's subdomains; this requires `url-subdomains-v1`. ip addresses
still match exactly. a search can carry project text in
its query, so allowing every search is a choice to make deliberately.

fetch rules also decide plain `curl` and `wget` downloads in shell commands.
with the `docs` rule above and a writable project folder,
`curl -fss -o guide.html https://docs.example.com/guide` is allowed: shield
checks the fetch against web rules and the output file against file rules.
this covers get and head requests with literal urls (up to 64 for curl, one for
wget), inspection options
such as `-fssl`, timeouts, retries and `-o` for curl, and `-q`, `--spider` and `-o` for
wget. wget must also pass `--no-hsts`, because otherwise it rewrites
`~/.wget-hsts`; without `-o` or `--spider` it is excluded. curl long-option values
must be separate arguments, such as `--output guide.html`; wget also accepts
`--output-document=guide.html`. curl's `-g`/`--get` also accepts repeated inline
`--data-urlencode` values in any option order, including `name=value`, `=value`
and bare content. shield evaluates the url with its encoded query included.
`@file`, `name@file` and `@-` inputs stay outside this fetch model, as do data
values without `-g` (which send a request body). uploads, request
bodies, headers, credentials, cookies, proxies, configuration files (including
an existing `~/.curlrc`, `~/.wgetrc`, or `~/.netrc` for wget without
`--no-netrc`) and other options leave the command to
your argv rules, as do explicit argv rules for curl or wget. fetches carry
`client` (`agent` for webfetch and codex opens, `shell` for curl and wget) and,
for shell clients, `redirects` (`follow` or `none`), so a rule can cover only
one of them. every url in a curl batch must pass web policy; one denied host
blocks the command. a single `-o` applies to the first url, with later bodies
going to stdout, following [curl's output rules](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--output).
repeated output options, mixed `--url` and positional urls, and `--next` remain
outside this model.

for example:

```yaml
- id: docs-downloads
  decision: allow
  conditions:
    domain: web
    action: fetch
    url: {schemes: [https], hosts: [docs.example.com]}
    request_fields: {/client: {exact: shell}}
```

for local smoke tests, restrict shell fetches to loopback hosts and require
redirects to be disabled. this keeps a localhost url from granting permission
to follow a redirect to another host:

```yaml
- id: local-smoke-tests
  decision: allow
  conditions:
    domain: web
    action: fetch
    url: {schemes: [http, https], hosts: [localhost, "127.0.0.1", "[::1]"], subdomains: true}
    request_fields:
      /client: {exact: shell}
      /redirects: {exact: none}
```

ordinary curl get/head requests match this rule. `curl -l` and wget requests
that follow redirects require another matching rule or approval.
this includes service names such as `auth.workspace.localhost` on every port.
shield's generated localhost suggestion uses this same scope and requires
`url-subdomains-v1` in the custom document's capabilities.

when a modeled fetch needs permission, shield returns it to the agent before
execution and directs it to open a reusable domain review with `policy_apply`.
the draft covers http and https, all paths, query strings and ports, and the
site's subdomains. shield uses a bundled public suffix list to choose the site:
`api.example.co.uk` suggests `example.co.uk`; `alice.github.io` stays separate
from `bob.github.io`. ip addresses remain exact. all localhost service names
share the local-server draft above. existing explicit policy rules still decide
their matching requests, and a configured automatic ask fallback still applies.

review the proposed scope before confirming it. preparing a proposal grants
nothing. if you choose not to save permission, the agent can request exact
one-time approval through `request_approve`; that does not save a domain rule.
shield offers saving once per domain, agent and session. declining, dismissing
or cancelling the confirmation suppresses further save offers for that domain
in the session, including after reconnecting, and the agent cannot propose any
other allow rule for that domain in that session, even a narrower one. to add
one anyway, run `shield rule add` yourself. later requests still follow
policy and can need one-time approval. a new session can offer saving again.

## directory options

many tools take an option that only says where to work, such as
`npm --prefix dir`, `git -c dir` or `make -c dir`. a pack or your project's
rules can declare such an option under `directory_options`, with the
`directory-options-v1` capability. when no rule decides a command as written,
shield then matches it as the same command without the option, run from that
folder. with this declaration and rule, `npm start`, `npm --prefix . start` and
`npm --prefix /path/to/project start` from any folder are all allowed, and
`npm --prefix /somewhere/else start` is not:

```yaml
directory_options:
  - {executable: npm, option: --prefix, position: anywhere, paths: follow}
rules:
  - id: npm-start
    decision: allow
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: npm
      arguments: {kind: exact, values: [start]}
      cwd: {within: {root: project}}
```

`paths` is required: `follow` when the tool resolves other relative paths
against the chosen folder, `unchanged` when it does not, as with
`cargo --manifest-path`; then only a folder equal to the current one is
normalized. an option whose value names a file, such as a manifest, sets
`value: file` and lists the default names in `files` (`files: [cargo.toml]`);
a value naming any other file leaves the command as written. other fields set
the value forms, position and how repeats combine:

| field | values and default |
| --- | --- |
| `forms` | `separate`, `equals`, `attached`; long options default to separate/equals, short options to separate/attached. attached values require a single-letter short option. |
| `position` | `leading` (default) or `anywhere` before `--`. |
| `value` | `directory` (default) or `file`; file values require `files`. |
| `repeat` | `refuse` (default), `last`, or `chain` to resolve each relative value against the previous one. |
| `paths` | required: `follow` or `unchanged`. |

a rule written for the command as typed keeps deciding it. values with
`~`, `$` or backquotes left after shell analysis, missing values and undeclared
forms leave the command as written.

unknown keys, source nulls, duplicate keys, and unsupported schemas are rejected.
see the [rule reference](rule-reference.md) for fields and capabilities.
policy comparisons outside the finite literal model report incomplete.

## pack variables, preconditions and templates

a pack can declare typed `variables` that each project sets for its own
selection, such as a package manager or a cloud profile. a rule or precondition
uses `{var: name}` wherever a text selector is accepted, and `when` tests switch
entries on for particular values. shield fills in values when it prepares the
policy, so hooks evaluate ordinary literal rules. an entry that refers to a
variable without a value is inactive: unset means no check.

`preconditions` gate the whole pack. when a precondition's conditions match and
none of its `requires_any` objects holds, the pack answers with its `on_unmet`
ask or deny, even if a more specific pack rule would allow the request. when one
object holds, the pack's ordinary rules decide as usual. a precondition never
allows anything. in packs that declare `templates-v1`, reasons, guidance and
`on_unmet` text can include `{{name}}`, which is replaced by the value.

```yaml
capabilities: [structured-rules-v1, argument-rules-v1, variables-v1, preconditions-v1, templates-v1]
variables:
  package_manager:
    type: choice
    description: package manager agents use
    values: [npm, pnpm, yarn]
    suggest: [{file: pnpm-lock.yaml, value: pnpm}]
preconditions:
  - id: package-manager
    conditions: {domain: argv, executable: {one_of: [npm, pnpm, yarn]}, arguments: {kind: any}}
    requires_any:
      - executable: {var: package_manager}
    on_unmet:
      decision: deny
      message: this project uses {{package_manager}}.
rules:
  - id: npx-with-pnpm
    when: [{var: package_manager, equals: pnpm}]
    conditions: {domain: argv, executable: npx, arguments: {kind: any}}
    decision: deny
```

variable types are `choice`, `string`, `list`, `boolean` and `path`. use `choice`
with `values` for a fixed selection, `string` for text, `list` for several text
values, `boolean` for conditional activation, and `path` for a location.
each declaration includes a `description`; `required` and `default` control
whether the project must supply a value. see
[pack configuration](local-registry.md#pack-variables-and-rule-overrides) for
setting values without editing the pack.

variables are also the pack's setup flow: `shield pack add` asks one question per
variable in the order the pack declares them. an optional `setup` object words
the question. `question` replaces the description as the question text,
`unset` labels the answer that leaves an optional variable unset, and `value`
and `placeholder` label the typed row of a string, path or free-text list.
`ask_when` takes `when` tests on variables declared earlier and asks only when
they hold:

```yaml
variables:
  profile:
    type: string
    description: read-only profile agents must use
    layer: local
    setup:
      question: allow log filtering only with a specific profile?
      unset: any profile (no check)
      value: only this profile
      placeholder: acme-read-only
  region:
    type: string
    description: region agents must use with that profile
    setup:
      unset: any region
      value: only this region
      ask_when: [{var: profile, set: true}]
```

a skipped question keeps the variable's current value. a required variable
without a default cannot use `unset` or `ask_when`.

### parts of a variable

a pack can use one string setting for a compound cli name and its separate mcp
fields. with `variable-parts-v1`, this text selector selects a zero-based component:

```yaml
fields:
  /owner: {text: {var: repository, split: {separator: /, index: 0}}}
  /repo: {text: {var: repository, split: {separator: /, index: 1}}}
```

for `repository: acme/web`, the fields must equal `acme` and `web`. the result is
literal text, never a pattern. declare a string `match` constraint to require the
complete setting's shape. separators contain 1–16 bytes without nul; indexes are
0–15. missing or empty selected parts refuse preparation. an unset setting leaves
the referencing entry inactive, as with ordinary variable selectors. parts apply
to string and choice settings, and to lists inside a precondition's
`requires_any` ([several values](#several-values-in-one-check)); booleans and
paths cannot be split.

### prefixes built from a variable

a setting is often one piece of a longer argument, such as the repository in a
github api path. with `variable-prefixes-v1`, a `prefix` text selector can list
parts: literal text and string or choice `{var}` references, including `split`
parts. shield joins them into one literal prefix when it prepares the pack:

```yaml
arguments:
  kind: options
  prefix: [api]
  flags: [--paginate]
  values: []
  operands: {match: {prefix: [repos/, {var: repository}, /]}, min: 1, max: 1}
```

for `repository: acme/web`, the operand must start with `repos/acme/web/`; end the
parts with a separator so `repos/acme/web-other/` does not match. the joined text
is never a pattern. a part list holds 1–16 parts and at least one reference; an
unset reference leaves the entry inactive. booleans and paths cannot be parts;
lists can inside a precondition's `requires_any`, described next.

### several values in one check

a project often works with more than one value of a setting, such as a fork and
its upstream repository. declare the setting as a list of strings and project it
inside a precondition's `requires_any`. with `variable-list-branches-v1`, shield
repeats each branch that splits a list or uses it as a prefix part once per
item, so every part in one copy comes from the same item:

```yaml
variables:
  repository:
    type: list
    description: exact owner/repo values
    items: {type: string, match: {regex: "[a-za-z0-9-]+/[a-za-z0-9_.-]+"}}
    max_items: 8
preconditions:
  - id: repository-scope
    conditions: {domain: mcp, server: github, tool: {glob: "*"}}
    requires_any:
      - fields:
          /owner: {text: {var: repository, split: {separator: /, index: 0}}}
          /repo: {text: {var: repository, split: {separator: /, index: 1}}}
    on_unmet: {decision: deny, message: "use one of {{repository}}."}
```

for `repository: [acme/web, example/web-fork]`, a request for `acme` and `web`
or for `example` and `web-fork` passes; `acme` with `web-fork` is denied because
no single item supplies both parts. each copy counts toward the 16
`requires_any` alternatives at the list's `max_items`, so declare a `max_items`
that fits. rules and precondition `conditions` cannot split a list or use it as
a prefix part. a single string written for a list setting is a one-item list,
so changing a setting from a string to a list keeps existing bindings.

### optional checks

a `{var}` reference turns its whole entry off while the variable is unset. to
keep the rule and drop only one check instead, an option grammar accepts two
forms:

- `match: {var: name, unset: any}` on a valued option accepts any value while
  `name` is unset, and only the bound value once it is set.
- an item of `require_all`, `require_any` or `forbid` can be
  `{name: option, when: [tests]}`; the option is listed only while the tests hold.

with these, one rule allows `aws logs filter-log-events` with any profile and
region until the project sets them, then requires each value that is set:

```yaml
  - id: logs-filter
    decision: allow
    agents:
      codex:
        prefixes:
          - [aws, logs, filter-log-events]
    conditions:
      domain: argv
      executable: aws
      arguments:
        kind: options
        leading: {flags: [], values: [--profile, --region]}
        prefix: [logs, filter-log-events]
        flags: []
        values: [--profile, --region, --log-group-name, --filter-pattern]
        operands: false
    requirements:
      arguments:
        kind: options
        leading:
          flags: []
          values:
            - {name: --profile, match: {var: profile, unset: any}}
            - {name: --region, match: {var: region, unset: any}}
        prefix: [logs, filter-log-events]
        flags: []
        values:
          - {name: --profile, match: {var: profile, unset: any}}
          - {name: --region, match: {var: region, unset: any}}
          - --log-group-name
          - --filter-pattern
        operands: false
        require_all:
          - {name: --profile, when: [{var: profile, set: true}]}
          - {name: --region, when: [{var: region, set: true}]}
    on_unmet:
      decision: deny
```

the rule has no `message`, because a template naming an unset variable would
turn the rule off. agents are told what failed instead, for example
`--profile must be acme-read-only.` or `missing required option: --profile.`

shield checks a pack's rules with every conditional item listed, whatever its
`when` tests. an option that one item requires and another forbids is refused
even when their tests can never hold together.

### codex prefix rules

`agents.codex.prefixes`, which needs the `agent-outputs-v1` capability, lists
the command prefixes codex may run outside its sandbox. that matters for
commands such as `aws` that need the network. while the rule is active and
allows, shield writes each prefix to `.codex/rules/shield.rules`. a position can
list alternatives:

```yaml
    agents:
      codex:
        prefixes:
          - [aws, logs, filter-log-events]
          - [aws, logs, [tail, get-log-events]]
```

each prefix must start with the rule's own executable and argument prefix, and
may add tokens after it. a rule matching `aws logs` can list
`[aws, logs, tail]` but not `[aws]` or `[aws, s3]`. the rule's executable and
argument prefix must be literals or a `one_of` of literals.

shield's hooks still decide every command. when policy asks about a command
whose every part matches one of these prefixes, such as
`aws logs tail --follow`, the hook blocks it even under the allow fallback,
because codex would otherwise run it without asking. a command behind a wrapper
such as `env` or inside `bash -c` keeps codex's sandbox and follows the
fallback. turning the rule off, changing its
decision or failing its `when` removes the prefix the next time shield writes the policy files or runs setup.
see [project setup](claude-project.md) for when the file is written.
`shield rule list --json` reports, for each entry that depends on variables or is
overridden, the values it used and the resolved rule, or why it is inactive.
invalid variable references and templates report the owning entry and field,
the relevant variable names and the selected pack when available. use that
location to correct the source or binding. these errors omit configured values;
an oversized rendered message identifies its field and variables without
printing the rendered text.
project custom rules do not accept variables, `when` or templates.

## share rule bodies in a pack

packs can share one rule body across commands. project custom rules use
independent rules.

declare `invocations` and `command_sets` on the pack, then reference them from
a rule. they require `invocation-groups-v1` and `command-sets-v1` respectively.
this pack fragment shares an inspection body between two commands and two
leading argument forms:

```yaml
invocations:
  globals: {id_prefix: v, segments: [[[], [--plain]]]}
command_sets:
  inspection: {status: base-status, diff: base-diff}
rules:
  - id: inspection
    invocation: globals
    command_set: inspection
    conditions: {domain: argv, executable: acme, arguments: {kind: any}}
    decision: allow
```

the `acme --plain status` match has id `v1-base-status`. requirements inspect the
complete original argv. groups declare finite exact vectors; they do not guess
global options or strip unknown arguments. each command set belongs to one rule
body. `shield rule list --json` includes shared definitions alongside canonical bodies;
an exact matched `rule_ref` returns its complete argument condition. human pack
summaries count stored bodies, invocation groups and command members separately.

## reading shield's documentation

the executable bundles every markdown page under shield's `docs/` directory at
build time, including nested pages. the bundle is compressed and decoded in
memory by shield; no external decompressor is needed. these tools work offline
and return the binary's version; they do not read project files or fetch online documentation.
page paths are relative to that directory, such as `policy-rules.md`.

fresh integrations approve the documentation tools without asking by default.
existing integrations keep their saved tool approvals. after installing a build
with additional tools, rerun `shield mcp setup --agent codex` or `shield mcp setup --agent claude` and
mark the documentation tools on the tool permissions page, then restart the
agent session. rerunning setup preserves saved selections until you change them.

- `docs_list`: list page paths, titles and line counts. optional `cursor`
  continues a page; `limit` is 1–100, default 50. continue with `next_cursor`.
- `docs_search`: find case-insensitive literal `query` text in the guides.
  the query matches within one line: `.*` and `[` match themselves, surrounding
  spaces are significant, and a query must be 1–1024 bytes, not only whitespace
  and without line breaks. optional `path` selects one listed page. results
  contain `path`, one-based `line` and the matching line's `text` without its
  line break, in path and line order. use `cursor` and `limit` as for listing;
  continue with `next_cursor` and the same query and path.
- `docs_read`: read a listed `path`, optionally continuing with `cursor`. `limit` is 1–400 lines, default 100. the result includes
  `content`, `total_lines` and `next_cursor` for continuation. `content`
  holds the lines exactly as stored, line breaks included, so joining the
  `content` of successive reads reproduces the page.

`limit` is a maximum: a result also ends early at 256 kib of serialized rows or line strings,
so continue from `next_cursor` until it is null.
every result includes `version`, the shield version whose guides it returns.
unknown arguments are refused.

an unknown page returns `not_found` and directs the agent to `docs_list`;
these are exact catalog paths, not filesystem paths, so `../readme.md` or a
differently cased name is not found. searches with no matches return an empty
list. cursors bind the tool, filters and exact bundle digest. keep filters
unchanged; `invalid_cursor` means restart without a cursor. search omits `total`
and stops at the page boundary; a conservative cursor may lead to an empty final
page. a first item larger than the page budget is returned alone within transport
bounds. reads without a cursor begin at line 1.

when the custom-rules skill's examples do not cover a command's grammar,
`docs_search` finds the matching guide and its examples. inspect the current
rules with `rule_list` so reviewed variants can extend an existing custom rule.

## bundled skills and prompts

the server advertises the mcp skills extension for modern clients, which use
mcp `2026-07-28` per-request metadata. for example, send this
newline-delimited request to the registered server:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"skills/list","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolversion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientcapabilities":{}}}}
```

the list names each bundled skill and its files; the tools and documentation
work without activating any of them. each skill is served at
`skill://shield/<name>/skill.md`, and each change it proposes still needs your
approval in the form:

- `project-setup`: initialize shield, connect agents or hub, enable enforcement
  and check setup; configure additional permission packs and rules when requested.
  for requested permission configuration, it reads each package's development
  commands and checks what each one runs,
  then asks you to approve two changes: the packs that match the project's
  tools, and project rules for the development commands no pack covers, listed
  one line per command. it only adds, and anything it leaves out keeps asking.
- `custom-rules`: your agent writes a project rule when shield keeps asking
  about work that will come up again, or when you ask to allow, block or always
  ask about something.
- `policy-audit`: ask your agent to audit or clean up the project's policy. it
  finds expired, unused and redundant custom rules, packs the project no longer
  uses and overrides that repeat or loosen a pack, and flags a custom rule as
  dangerous only with a concrete harmful command it allows. it lists the
  findings, then proposes removing or narrowing them in one change. rule use
  comes from this machine's request history, so it keeps rules that look
  unused but whose target still exists.
- `pack-update`: ask your agent to update the installed packs. it refreshes
  release metadata, prepares one on-demand update of installed packs, including
  pins, and tells you each version change and which commands now decide
  differently before you approve it. profiles and pin modes are preserved at the
  reviewed versions. a release that needs a newer shield is reported rather than
  installed; no pack updates automatically.

the server also publishes the `install_pack` prompt through
`prompts/list` and `prompts/get`. discovery and reads return private cache
scope and zero ttl.

to expose only the static bundle without an enrolled project, launch
