preparation, including for tasks-capable calls. host presentation of tasks depends on the client.

### operation progress

mcp clients can include `_meta.progresstoken` in `tools/call` parameters to
receive `notifications/progress` while shield acquires registry content or
compares policy. tokens may be strings or integers. for example:

```json
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":7,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"pack_info","arguments":{"reference":"main/canonic/node"},"_meta":{"progresstoken":"pack-review-7"}}}
```

messages identify stages such as reading and verifying the registry catalog,
release history or pack artifact, preparing policy inputs, comparing permissions
and preparing a review. registry enrollment can report identity/key
discovery before its separate trust confirmation. stage messages contain no
registry urls, command text, settings or credentials.

the increasing `progress` value counts stages within that rpc; it is not a
percentage, and shield omits `total`. at most 64 stages are offered per rpc.
legacy settings forms retain the count after input; modern input retries are
new rpcs with their own tokens and counts. calls without a token send no progress.

progress is best effort: queue pressure or request completion can drop stages.
notifications never follow the request's final reply. use the final tool result
to determine the outcome. progress cannot approve a proposal, extend
a deadline or revive a cancelled operation. whether a host displays notifications
depends on that host.

### client startup

shield exposes project inspection, approved policy changes, and diagnostic
evaluation over stdio using mcp `2025-06-18`, `2025-11-25`, and per-request
`2026-07-28`. other clients can
launch `shield mcp serve --project /workspace/acme` explicitly, replacing
the example path with the selected project. a project without policy starts with
in-session initialization available. startup failure exits 1 with a
fixed stderr diagnostic and empty stdout.
launch from the selected project's directory. shield serves the nearest
configured project holding the agent's session folder, or else its working
directory; `--project` applies only when no configured project holds that
folder. a moved, copied or worktree folder therefore serves itself.

a launch may supply an agent and an explicitly mapped host session through
internal registration arguments; tool input cannot appoint either. client names
are declarations. shield generates a new connection id on each launch.

the client initializes with a supported protocol version, sends
`notifications/initialized`, then uses `tools/list` or `tools/call`. the server
supports ping and cancellation and advertises tools, resources and prompts.
`skills/*` requires modern metadata. every tool publishes
strict input and output schemas, with authority annotations. shield echoes a
supported requested version. for other version strings it offers `2025-11-25`;
the client decides whether it supports that version.

### result format and limits

for compact packs, `rule_list` lists canonical rule bodies. its optional
`shared` array includes each pack selector, invocation groups and command sets.
bindings are pack-only source fields. for a rule present in the active policy,
a `rule_ref` selects the materialized rule, including its matched leading
arguments and command member, without listing every invocation combination.
pass the evaluation's `candidate_id` with `rule_ref` to inspect that exact retained
snapshot, including an old active generation or pending proposal. omitting the
handle selects active policy at lookup time. lists also accept `candidate_id`;
preserve it with the other arguments when following `next_cursor`. exact rule
selection accepts the handle but no paging arguments. an unavailable handle
returns `candidate_unavailable` without selecting another snapshot.
custom-rule inspection includes shared and local rules;
a local rule with a shared rule's id replaces it in lists and exact lookups.
inspection uses the same strict source parser and budgets
as policy admission.

### read a proposal's full reports

proposal results and `policy_show` include `report_resources` with two addresses:
the captured policy comparison and the retained review evidence. exact proposal
results also include mcp `resource_link` blocks. text-only clients can read the
same addresses from text block 1. use mcp `resources/read` with the returned uri:

```json
{"uri":"copy_the_returned_report_uri"}
```

the json comparison report preserves coverage, unknowns and before/after
evidence. the evidence report includes attribution, reasons, linked requests,
current disposition and outcome, and any authorization events. private
connection settings and secrets are redacted. a report is inspection only;
apply a change through its separate, unchanged `apply_arguments` and host
confirmation.

report addresses belong to one enrolled project and exact proposal candidate.
they can be read after reconnect while the proposal remains retained. evidence
reflects its latest retained disposition; a uri never switches to a different
candidate or project. a foreign, unknown or reclaimed report returns a resource
not-found error. discover the address shape with `resources/templates/list`;
`resources/list` continues to list bundled static resources. reports exceeding
the response limit return an error rather than partial evidence. project reports
are unavailable on the project-free static server.

### tool result format

results retain the complete envelope in `structuredcontent`. text block 0 gives
short guidance; text block 1 is bounded json with `data`, `error`, `missing` and
`truncated`. inspection tools include requested data there. proposal/withdrawal
text includes ids, status, candidate handles and report addresses; use the report
links or `policy_show` to inspect the proposal. text-only clients parse block 1
rather than block 0. the shared
envelope has schema_version, project_id, nullable policy_revision, data, missing,
truncated and nullable error. allow/ask/deny diagnostics are successful results.
failures set `iserror` and use fixed safe codes/messages with an applicable operator
route. secrets are redacted from exposed evidence; credentials cannot be embedded
in project rule conditions.

json-rpc framing uses newline-delimited utf-8, with no batches or content-length
headers. duplicate decoded keys, nuls, positional parameters, invalid ids and
unknown fields refuse. arguments that do not match a tool's input schema return
an `invalid_input` tool result. frames are limited to 524,288 bytes plus the
newline; responses to 4 mib plus newline. pages have a 256 kib serialized-items
budget and end early when it is reached. each connection's snapshot handles
may pin up to 1 gib of source and compiled bytes, enough for the largest bundle
and plan that policy limits allow. cursors retain no result data. pending-review captures
remain protected. a session accepts at most 1,024 inbound messages; the next one
ends it with `-32000` "session message limit reached".

one worker processes tool calls in arrival order while the dispatcher handles
input and ping. at most 64 tool calls may be outstanding, including queued calls
and any legacy call waiting for confirmation. additional calls receive `-32000`.
duplicate outstanding ids close the session.
bundled reads use a separate worker with eight outstanding reads, allowing them
to finish while the policy evaluator is busy.
task management uses two separate workers with eight outstanding requests, so
status and cancellation remain reachable while preparation runs.
`--request-timeout-ms` bounds active evaluation and encoding from dispatch
(default 5,000 ms, range 1–60,000). a call that exceeds it receives `-32001`
with recovery guidance. queued calls have no separate deadline and wait for
the worker to return. client cancellation suppresses pending responses.
a legacy approval form pauses the call's budget while the person decides. its
continuation uses the remaining budget for revalidation, commit and encoding.
modern form continuations arrive as separate calls with their own budgets.
cancellation is cooperative, so a worker blocked in native i/o can continue
to hold up the queue after its timeout reply. clients also own process and i/o
limits. lost `policy_propose` replies can be recovered by resubmitting the same
arguments. for any lost `pack_add` or `pack_configure` reply, inspect `policy_show`
before retrying, even if no form opened. consumed form state cannot be replayed
and private answers must not be reconstructed.

keep stdin open until you have the replies you need. when it closes, queued
`policy_propose`, `pack_add`, `pack_configure`, `pack_update`, `pack_remove`, `policy_withdraw` and `policy_apply`
calls are refused with `-32800` and never run, a pending confirmation is
withdrawn, and read-only tools still finish.

closing stdin drains admitted work and joins the worker before exit 0. framing or
transport failure cancels and joins work and exits 1. resident clients complete
each call from its correlated envelope; process exit supplies no missing result or
permission. native blocking stdin readers end at process exit after early failure.

native macos tests and pinned official sdk fixtures exercise this interface; live-agent
setup and linux/windows runtime coverage remain separate validation work.

project policy, approvals and history # project policy, approvals and history

use this guide to manage an initialized project: inspect policy, connect agents,
review changes, and investigate requests. if this is your first setup, follow
[your first project](getting-started.md) first. for the meaning of allow, ask,
and deny, read [policy decisions](policy-decisions.md).

## choose a task

| you want to… | start with |
| --- | --- |
| see what is active | `shield status`; use `shield doctor` for a problem. |
| pause or resume native checks | [pause or resume shield](#pause-or-resume-shield) |
| connect or repair an agent | [native hooks and mcp setup](#native-hooks-and-mcp-setup) |
| add a reusable permission pack | [find and install a pack](local-registry.md#find-and-install-a-pack) |
| change one project-specific permission | [custom rules](#custom-rules-and-proposed-changes) |
| review a change prepared by an agent | `shield policy review`, or the host's shield approval prompt. |
| let location rules include another directory | [additional access paths](#additional-access-paths) |
| understand a past request | [request history](#request-history) |

inspection commands report state. commands that change policy show a review
and require confirmation. the examples below run from your project directory;
replace illustrative ids and paths with values from your own project.

## inspect your project

run shield in a project directory, or add `--project /path/to/acme`. inspection
finds the nearest enrolled ancestor; a nearer enrollment owns its own boundary.

```sh
shield status
shield doctor
shield policy show --json
shield rule list --json
```

`status` is the everyday overview. use `doctor` when something looks wrong: it
checks the policy files, registry checkpoints, pack artifacts, and the
binary your agents run, and gives repair commands when needed. json output
provides full structured details for scripts and agents.

status and doctor can inspect a validated historical checkpoint without saving
its conversion. `checkpoint_upgrade_pending: true` reports that the upgrade is
still unsaved. if the review directory is read-only or the disk is full, restore
write access or free space before retrying the operation. hooks and changes
require the conversion to be saved before proceeding.

doctor distinguishes agent integration repair (`shield mcp setup`) from
problems in the policy files, which `policy_files.error` names; fix those in
the files. follow the command for the reported problem.

## pause or resume shield

```sh
shield disable
shield enable
shield status
```

each change shows a review and requires confirmation in your terminal. agents
can request the same change with `disable {}` or `enable {}`;
shield shows you a confirmation form and changes the setting only if you accept.
json mode and redirected input cannot confirm it.

the command writes `enforcement: paused` or `enabled` to your uncommitted
`.shield/config.local.yml`, so other developers keep their own setting; a value
committed in `config.yml` applies to everyone who has not set their own. see
[settings](policy-files.md#settings). policy, packs, history, grants and agent
registrations remain in place. `status` and `doctor` report whether
shield is enabled.

while disabled, native hooks retain protected-file and operator-command guards.
agents cannot use the pause to edit runtime state, forge grants or invoke the
operator cli. saved protected-file allow choices remain in force; other
protected accesses are blocked during the pause. shell requests
must have a verifiable protected footprint; unsupported or incomplete analysis
is blocked. other requests return no permission decision and follow your
agent's own permissions and sandbox. project rules are not applied, and
shield records no native request history during this pause.
its mcp tools remain available, with human confirmation still required for
administrative changes. explicit checked runs and sdk consumers continue to
enforce policy.

hooks inspect submitted requests; they do not isolate same-user processes or
authenticate edits made outside interception. the enable review makes explicit
that resuming applies the policy files as they are, including any edits made
while paused.

disabling removes shield-generated codex permission rules; enabling restores
them from the policy files. restart connected agents when the result requests it,
so they refresh cached rules. native hooks read the setting on their next
invocation; a toggle does not cancel requests already underway. enabling
requires readable policy files. if restoring permission rules needs repair,
checks are already enabled and the result names `shield mcp setup`.

## initialize or revisit setup

run `shield init` to review and confirm project policy. it offers the same
guided agent setup as `shield mcp setup`. mark the agents to configure, or continue
with none selected. `--agent claude` or `--agent codex`, repeatable, selects
directly; `--no-setup` skips agent setup.

new projects acquire the signed main baseline with recommended preselected.
choose another profile during setup, pass `--profile strict`, or use
`--no-baseline` to skip it. download or verification failure leaves a new
project unenrolled. offline setup can use `--no-baseline` with supplied artifacts.

existing packs, rules, profiles, and removals are preserved. use
`shield pack remove baseline` for later removal. see
[terminal controls](operator-experience.md).

## native hooks and mcp setup

add the agent you want to use, then restart and trust it:

```sh
shield mcp setup --agent claude
shield mcp setup --agent codex
```

each command installs hooks and mcp while keeping the other agent registered.
`shield mcp setup` without `--agent` asks which agents to install or repair, or
resumes an interrupted confirmed plan. `shield mcp setup --remove` asks which
agents to remove, or takes `--agent`, and preserves policy, approvals, and
history. add `--dry-run` to see the review without writing anything. edited owned entries report a conflict rather than
being overwritten.

in an agent session, setup uses shield's `mcp_setup` confirmation forms. a large
administrative review is presented in numbered pages without omitting contents.
accepting an intermediate page applies nothing. the agent repeats the same call
using the returned `retry_arguments` to show the next page. only acceptance of
the final page applies the complete change, after checking that the reviewed
files are still current. declining or cancelling any page discards that review.
an unanswered review stays open until you answer it or the agent session's
connection ends.

new codex setups let valid ask requests proceed by default, including unmatched
requests and strict-profile asks. existing block or allow choices are preserved;
there is no block picker or flag. deny, protected files, and invalid mapped requests
still block. unmodeled internal tools defer to codex permissions. codex's own
sandbox and approvals also apply.

status and doctor report the effective ask fallback. missing authorization or
an interrupted setup can report block; finish the plan with `shield mcp setup`.
see [ask handling](policy-decisions.md#what-happens-after-ask) and the
[integration guide](claude-project.md) for loading and coverage.

## protected files

```sh
shield protection set
```

when policy checks are enabled, native hooks ask by default before agents read
`.mcp.json` and agent hook settings (`.claude/settings.local.json`,
`.claude/settings.json`, `.codex/hooks.json`, `.codex/config.toml`),
which may hold credentials, and block agents from changing them. direct edits
to `.shield` policy files stay blocked: agents propose policy edits, or request
exact approval for a supported git restoration as described below.

the same settings protection covers the adapter's configured agent home,
including a relocated home. verified session-output reads retain their separate
scope; they do not permit configuration writes.

git merges, branch switches and other tree-changing commands also check protected
agent settings. a change to files such as `.codex/config.toml` requires separate
review unless changing agent settings is allowed; a session grant does not
override that check.

`protection set` asks about each group and confirms the result:

| group | default | other choice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| reading agent settings | ask, or block where the agent cannot prompt | allow without asking |
| changing agent settings | block | allow; the agent can then remove shield's hooks or the host confirmation that mcp policy changes rely on |

reading agent settings includes commands whose output can print them without
naming them, such as `git show head:.mcp.json`, an unscoped `git diff` or
`git log -p`, `git grep`, and `grep -r` over a folder that holds them. add a
pathspec that leaves settings out, as in `git diff -- src`, to keep such a
command out of this group. listing names and metadata, as `ls`, `find`,
`git ls-files` and `git status` do, is not reading; `git ls-files --stage`,
`git status --porcelain=v2` and `git status -v` are, because they print object ids
or changes. the same footprint check applies when those commands omit paths.
unknown git subcommands can be aliases or external commands, so their output
conservatively reaches repository settings. explicit `-c` or `--config-env`
overrides of `alias.*`, `core.pager` or `diff.external` use that same footprint.
git option values do not narrow this footprint: in
`git diff --ignore-matching-lines src`, `src` is a regular expression, so the
diff can include settings outside that folder. unknown option arity also keeps
the complete footprint rather than guessing which words are paths.

git protection follows the worktree the command actually targets, including
linked worktrees and separate repository entry folders. when running git from
an entry folder, use root-relative pathspecs such as `git diff -- :/src` to select
files from its worktree root. both settings symlinks and their targets remain
protected. if shield cannot establish the target root or the command overrides
repository selection, it keeps the conservative protection checks.

`.shield/state/`, compiled caches, the `.shield` folder itself and
`.shield/.gitignore` stay protected whatever you choose, and agents still cannot
run shield operator actions. direct policy-file writes remain blocked, in
`.shield/`, `.config/shield/` or a `--config` file's folder. help-only requests
follow ordinary policy. the choice is the `protection` setting, written to your
`config.local.yml`
([settings](policy-files.md#settings)); agents cannot change it. `status` lists
any group you have opened. an invalid `protection` value makes policy unavailable;
supported native requests then require exact in-session review until it is fixed.

### allowing one blocked request

if policy files contain conflict markers or another error, use `status` or
`doctor` to inspect the problem. supported native requests can still use
`request_approve` and an identical retry. the form explains that policy is
unavailable and warns about any settings or policy replacement. a supported git
restoration can repair a conflicted file this way; direct policy edits, runtime
state and caches stay protected. pending and approved native requests remain
usable under their existing expiry and exact-request checks.

if the agent also has no registered shield approval connection in this
checkout, repair the policy files yourself first, for example by resolving their
git conflicts in your terminal. then run `shield mcp setup` and restart the
agent session. setup also requires valid policy.

you don't need to change these settings to let an agent do one blocked thing.
when shield blocks a change to agent settings or policy files, a credentials
read the agent cannot ask about, a policy deny, a codex request that needs
approval, or a codex tool shield cannot check, the agent can ask you in the
same conversation. it calls shield's `request_approve` tool, and your agent
shows shield's form with the exact action, the folder, why shield blocked it
and what allowing it can do. if you accept, the agent repeats the identical
request once within five minutes; anything else is still blocked. approval
creates no standing permission. if you decline, the agent
continues without it.

a git merge, branch switch or other git operation that may replace shield's
policy files also offers this route when codex cannot ask at its hook. the form
warns that the command may change permissions or turn off protection. you approve
the exact submitted command once, including its options and working directory;
the git revision and resulting policy edit are not frozen or previewed. direct
file writes to shield policy still require a policy proposal.

for conflict resolution, supported `git checkout`, `git restore` and
`git checkout-index` forms can restore explicit files after `--`, including
policy files. for example, `git checkout --ours -- :/.mcp.json :/.shield/shield.lock`
can request review in a known worktree. source revisions, ours/theirs and
supported index restoration use the same route. the form names the actual target
worktree and warns about both policy and settings changes. accepting authorizes
one identical retry; changing the target or command needs fresh approval. broad
selections, unknown options, runtime state, caches and `.shield/.gitignore`
keep their protected boundary. git refs and file contents are not frozen by approval.

when one task needs several blocked requests, such as deleting the same branch
in two repositories, the agent can ask about up to eight of them in one form,
subject to a 12,000-byte limit for the complete confirmation. it should include
only requests still needed for the task. if a group is too long, shield approves
nothing and returns `retry_arguments` for a prefix that fits, plus
`remaining_request_ids` to review separately. each new call still needs your
confirmation. the agent can also ask about just one request, for example
`request_approve({"request_id":"hook-request-acme-1"})`, using an id from its refusal.
the form starts by saying how many one-time permissions accepting creates and
how many override a deny, change agent settings or may replace shield policy,
then shows each request in full. accepting allows each listed request once; the agent repeats each one
identically within five minutes, in any order. if any request in the group can
no longer be allowed, for example because it expired or your policy changed
while the form was open, nothing is allowed.

codex shows the form only when its approval policy allows prompts. if the
agent reports that it could not ask you, choose an approval policy that allows
prompts with `/permissions` in the same codex session; the agent then asks
again.

runtime state, caches, the `.shield` folder and its ignore file are never
offered, even once, and neither is a request that also touches them.

## custom rules and proposed changes

custom rules express project-specific permissions. for a worked example, see
[your first rule](policy-rules.md#your-first-rule).

### add, edit, or remove a custom rule

```sh
shield rule add
```

choose the matching form and decision, then review its scope. after confirming,
find the rule's id with `shield rule list --json`. to edit or remove a rule named
`inspect-status`, use the appropriate command:

```sh
shield rule edit inspect-status
shield rule remove inspect-status
```

the default **complete request** form binds normalized input, vendor fields,
cwd, environment, and executable. **exact command arguments** binds an executable
and argument array to the project cwd, with broader vendor/environment scope.
both ask for a decision, reason, and optional utc expiration. **structured rule**
accepts a complete rule in the [rule format](policy-rules.md).

editing shows the existing rule; empty answers preserve its conditions.
confirmation writes the validated change to the policy files; cancellation leaves
them unchanged.

### review an agent's proposal

agents can propose packs, rules, domain permissions, or folder access. check
whether a proposal covers one invocation or a broader set of requests. the agent
prepares the exact change and immediately requests approval in the conversation.
accept applies it; decline rejects it. cancellation, disconnection, a host that
gives up on the question, or the end of the agent session closes an unapplied
attempt. the end of a turn leaves it open, so the person can answer in the next
turn. changes to its base make it stale.
closed attempts cannot be accepted later.

for a direct operator review of a live change, run:

```sh
shield policy review
```

choose the live change explicitly. the review shows the change, agent's reason,
originating command, and permission comparison. tab opens the complete change,
including pack rules. choose accept, reject, or cancel review; cancellation
withdraws that attempt. there is no oldest-first approval queue.

agents can also submit a proposal's exact `apply_arguments` to
`policy_apply` for host approval. `policy_show` reads a proposal's outcome.
deferred work is saved as intent only when you request it, and needs fresh
preparation and approval when resumed.
see [mcp review](project-mcp.md#proposals-and-operator-review).
a proposal builds on the policy files as they are, including your hand edits,
and keeps them when applied.

changes to the policy files, setup or registry settings can invalidate
a proposal. ask the agent to prepare a fresh one, even if the policy revision
has not changed. independently confirmed protected-file settings remain current.
for successive proposals, wait for each result before preparing the next.

### edit the policy files by hand

the policy files are the policy. an edit to configuration or rules applies to
the next request; inspect `shield rule list --json` for the result, and
`shield status` for an error if the edit made the files invalid. use
`shield pack add` or `shield pack update` to acquire releases rather than
editing pack artifacts. see [policy files and settings](policy-files.md).

when shield writes a change, it preserves comments, blank lines, and layout outside changed entries.
removing a rule or pack also removes its preceding comments. if a change cannot
be made in place, such as reordering rules, shield rewrites below the opening
comments. the review identifies files that will be rewritten or lose comments.

## additional access paths

if your agent needs a reference folder outside the project, you can add that
folder to the roots used by location rules. adding a root does not itself allow
every operation there; the active rules still decide what the agent may do.

project configuration can bind reusable location rules to additional directories:

```yaml
access_paths:
  read: [/path/to/reference]
  write: [/path/to/scratch]
```

add this mapping to `.shield/config.yml`, preserving its `schema_version`, `packs`
and any `rules` selection; the next request uses it. an agent can also propose
one directory at a time with the mcp `access_path_add` change, which you
confirm in the host. these settings are retained
when installing, updating or removing packs and when changing custom rules.

rules with `{root: read}` use the project plus additional read and write roots;
`{root: write}` uses the project plus additional write roots. write access includes
read access. at most 64 additional native absolute directories are accepted;
duplicates within each list, traversal components, nuls, null lists and unknown
fields refuse. a configured root that does not exist when evaluated contains
nothing, so it leaves the union and the remaining roots still decide. exclusions
retain missing roots, protecting entries created through a containing root.
a root that exists but is not a directory, or cannot be inspected, makes its
location predicate unknown, and requests that depend on it are blocked.

native claude/codex integrations also include system temporary roots automatically
in these unions; no `access_paths` entry is needed for ordinary temporary files.
claude additionally supplies its verified current-session tool-result read scope.
these adapter observations are not stored in policy or accepted from diagnostic
tool input. explicit policy restrictions and protected-file checks still apply.

access paths bind policy predicates; the selected rules decide which operations
are permitted, including removal. they do not install a host filesystem sandbox.
native hook cwd remains inside the enrolled project; absolute operands can refer
to additional roots. protected shield/operator configuration remains guarded.

## action approvals

use this workflow only for stored requests from the restricted sdk text-read
integration or bounded native runner. to handle an ordinary claude or codex
permission prompt, use the host's approval flow. to change future permissions,
review a policy change instead. see
[approval scopes](policy-decisions.md#approving-a-request-versus-changing-policy).

```sh
shield request list
shield request show request
shield request approve request
shield request deny request
```

these commands cover restricted text-read and checked native requests together.
approval confirms one stored ask request for an exact retry, with a five-minute
grant. request resources, origin, project and active policy must still match.
policy denials cannot be approved. deny cancels a pending request or revokes an
unused grant. a consumed grant cannot authorize another execution.

read, checked-run and native-hook terminal outcomes remain available for up to ten minutes
within a separate bounded receipt store. repeating the original decision returns
the closed outcome without issuing permission. all-terminal groups can reconcile
without another form; approve only the live ids when a group mixes live and closed
requests. older or evicted ids report unavailable.
for native hooks, reporting a consumed outcome leaves its separate one-use
follow-up callback available for the original 60-second window. reporting never
renews that window or authorizes another execution. unreadable optional outcome
metadata stays preserved locally and unavailable; it does not prevent valid policy
or live grants from loading.

fresh approval requires a controlling terminal or the registered host's shield
confirmation form. redirected stdin, json flags and intercepted tool input do not
supply operator confirmation.

## request history

list requests, then copy an entry id into `shield history show entry`:

```sh
shield history list
shield history list --denied
shield history list --approved --agent claude
shield history show entry
```

agents use the `history_list` and `history_show` mcp tools. their optional
`project` argument can name the absolute root of an already enrolled worktree
inside this connection's project, for example:

```json
{"project":"/srv/acme/.gate/worktrees/feature","agent":"codex","denied":true}
```

this selects history for that read only. results identify the selected project,
and observation-page routes retain it. repeat the same project and filters for
cursor continuation. it does not change the connection's policy or approval
target, enroll a folder, or permit direct reads of `.shield/state`.
for a target outside the connection's project, connect shield in that target
project instead; the selector does not widen the connection's filesystem scope.

entries combine request decisions, operator decisions, and reported completion.
an identical native retry covered by a one-time approval is shown as approved
and allowed, with its original policy evaluation and the approval ids retained.
approval alone leaves execution unobserved. older records without an explicit
approval-to-retry link remain separate.
policy changes are recorded by the policy files themselves; use your version
control to see how they changed. `shield policy show` lists recent proposal
outcomes.

configuration changes are not request entries. shell entries show the submitted
source: the list shows its first line, and `show` prints the full command and
deciding rule. file entries show the action and path, such as
`write /srv/acme/app.js`.

a decision alone does not establish execution. completion without a reported
exit code stays without one; a blocked command is shown as not run. rewrite
refusals appear as `ask → blocked (rewrite required)`, with the explanation
and suggested form in the detail view.

### recording and retention

initialization retains up to 5,000 requests. the history action in
`shield policy review` changes the limit to 1–10,000, disables recording, or clears
optional history. clearing starts a new generation; increasing retention cannot
restore deleted records. policy and authorization records are separate, so
clearing history neither removes active policy nor restores consumed grants.

in an agent session, `history_configure` offers the same controls through a human
form. if the optional history lock's permissions have drifted, confirming a
control restores private permissions on the existing owned lock before applying
it. declining changes neither permissions nor settings. shield waits for a live
history writer and refuses linked, foreign or replaced lock files; it never
deletes a lock to force a control through. changing retention still requires
valid journal content. use the confirmed clear control to reset corrupt optional
history while preserving policy and grants.

history uses checksummed segments of at most 1 mib, capped at 64 mib per current
generation. recovery files, retention rewrites, and readers holding old files
can use more storage. segments reach stable storage on creation and when full;
a crash can lose buffered records from the current segment. observations can
be visible before their receipt is recorded.

on rotation, segments containing only requests beyond retention are removed.
at the storage cap, the oldest segments are removed even if their requests
are within retention. the list then reports `evicted_history` and may contain
fewer entries than the configured limit.

### completion links and missing data

completions link only to a retained allowed request or claude ask handed to
host approval with matching operation, agent, session, tool-call id, surface,
and cwd. without a shield reference, the complete host identity and operation
must identify exactly one request. missing identity or reused ids leave the
completion unlinked; matching command text alone is insufficient.

linking completion to ask preserves that decision and its prompt disposition.
it reports host execution, not individual operator approval. shell exit status
stays `unknown` without structured exit evidence.

displayed entries are limited to 8 kib; `truncated` and `missing` identify omitted
details. identical deliveries appear once. changed content under one delivery
id is marked `delivery_conflict`; torn writes are preserved as degraded history.
`status` reports unavailable optional history separately. expired and terminal
authorization request state is reclaimed independently.

## document format

shield accepts utf-8 json or a single yaml document using `schema_version: 1`.
keys must be strings. unknown fields, duplicate keys, unsupported capabilities,
and yaml anchors and aliases are rejected. omit optional source fields instead
of setting them to null; exact-request payloads can retain their supplied null
values. documents support no environment interpolation, command substitution,
or includes.

| field | project custom rules | permission pack |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | required integer `1`. | required integer `1`. |
| `kind` | required `custom`. | required `pack`. |
| `capabilities` | required list of exactly the capabilities used. | same. |
| `rules` | required array with unique rule ids; may be empty. | same. |
| `directory_options` | optional directory option declarations. | same. |
| `id`, `version` | not accepted. | required publisher/name and semantic release version. |
| `description`, `license`, `maintainers` | not accepted. | required nonempty description, license text, and nonempty maintainer list. |
| `engines` | not accepted. | required object containing only `shield`, with its supported semantic-version requirement. |
| `dependencies` | not accepted. | optional dependency declarations; see [packs](local-registry.md#pack-dependencies). |
| `variables`, `preconditions` | not accepted. | optional declarations; see [pack variables](policy-rules.md#pack-variables-preconditions-and-templates). |
| `invocations`, `command_sets` | not accepted. | optional shared bodies; see [rule reuse](policy-rules.md#share-rule-bodies-in-a-pack). |

project configuration selects the rule file. documents cannot select a project,
operator identity, or cache root. a saved edit applies to the next request.

## rule fields

| field | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | required stable identifier, unique within the document: 1–128 ascii bytes, beginning with a letter or digit, then letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `:`, or `-`. |
| `decision` | required `allow`, `ask`, or `deny`. pack rules may instead map all three profiles: `loose`, `recommended`, `strict`. |
| `conditions` | required object with a `domain` and the predicates that make this rule apply. |
| `requirements` | optional nonempty object of additional predicates, all of which must be verified for the successful decision. |
| `on_unmet` | required exactly when `requirements` is present; an `ask` or `deny` decision with optional `message` and `alternatives`. |
| `reason` | optional nonempty explanation, at most 4,096 utf-8 bytes. |
| `guidance` | optional successful-branch `message` and/or `alternatives`. |
| `expires_at` | optional quoted utc timestamp for custom rules; an expired rule contributes nothing. |
| `fallback` | pack-only `true`; lets this rule yield to regular decisions from other packs. |
| `invocation`, `command_set` | pack-only references to shared definitions; `command_set` requires `invocation`. |
| `when` | pack-only activation tests on declared variables. |
| `agents` | agent-specific outputs; see [codex prefix rules](policy-rules.md#codex-prefix-rules). |

guidance messages are at most 512 utf-8 bytes. alternatives contain one to three
nonempty strings, each at most 256 bytes. they suggest new requests to evaluate;
they do not authorize or rewrite the current request.

rule order does not determine precedence. see
[how rules combine](policy-decisions.md#how-rules-combine).

## text selectors

| shape | matches |
| --- | --- |
| `verify` or `{exact: verify}` | the complete literal field. |
| `{prefix: verify}` | text starting with `verify`. |
| `{one_of: [verify, report]}` | one of the listed literal values. |
| `{glob: '*.txt'}` | a glob against one field; `*` does not cross a path separator. |
| `{regex: 'get|describe'}` | a regex against the entire field, not a substring search. |
| `{not: {one_of: [prod, admin]}}` | a present value the inner selector does not match. |

selectors do not expand an argument into additional arguments. the shell command
`acme-check "two words"` has one argument containing a space, not two arguments.
glob and regex selectors require their respective capabilities; `not` requires
`negated-selectors-v1`. a `not` selector never matches a missing value, so pair
it with `require_all` when the option must be present.

## argument selectors

the `arguments` condition describes the arguments after the executable.

| `kind` | fields | use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `any` | no additional fields. | accept any argument list. |
| `exact` | `values`: literal string array. | match the complete argument list, including an empty list. |
| `prefix` | `values`: selector array; optional `leading` grammar. | match the start and leave the suffix unrestricted. leading options require `prefix-leading-v1`; `leading.interleaved: true` also accepts them between prefix words and requires `interleaved-leading-v1`. |
| `sequence` | `prefix`: selector array; `rest`: `none`, `any`, or `each`. | match initial tokens and constrain the rest. |
| `options` | `prefix`, `flags`, `values`, `operands`; optional parsing controls. | accept a declared operation and reviewed options. |
| `risk_tokens` | `prefix`, `any_of`. | detect restrictions conservatively; cannot grant allow. |

for a sequence, `rest: {kind: none}` rejects remaining arguments;
`rest: {kind: any}` accepts them. use
`rest: {kind: each, match: selector, min: n, max: n}` to constrain each remaining
argument. counts default to 0–256.

an options grammar distinguishes flags from options that consume a value:

```yaml
kind: options
prefix: [verify]
flags: [--verbose]
values: [--format]
operands: false
```

this fragment accepts `verify`, `verify --verbose`, and `verify --format json`.
it rejects `verify --format` and `verify report.txt`. it does not restrict the
format value to json; use `{name: --format, match: json}` in `values` for that.

declared options are optional unless required. unknown options fail matching.
use `require_all`, `require_any`, and `forbid` to check declared option names.
`leading: {flags: [...], values: [...]}` declares global options before the
operation. `operands` is `false`, `true`, or `{match: selector, min: n, max: n}`.
the `--` separator ends option parsing; subsequent tokens are operands.

some tools read global options anywhere, among options a rule cannot list.
`unknown_options: skip` passes over undeclared options so a grammar can still
check the declared ones; it needs `operands: true`. `long_abbreviations: true`
accepts any unique prefix of a declared long option, as argparse-based tools
do, so declare the tool's complete global option set when you use it. this
requirement accepts any aws command that names the `acme-ro` profile, written
in full or abbreviated, anywhere in the command:

```yaml
kind: options
prefix: []
flags: [--debug, --no-paginate, --no-verify-ssl, --no-sign-request]
values: [{name: --profile, match: acme-ro}, --region, --output, --query, --endpoint-url]
operands: true
unknown_options: skip
long_abbreviations: true
require_all: [--profile]
```

it allows `aws logs tail g --since 1h --prof acme-ro` and refuses
`aws s3 ls --profile acme-admin`. the settings require `unknown-options-v1` and
`option-abbreviations-v1`. skipping says nothing about what the skipped options
do, so allowances for specific operations keep their declared grammars.

with abbreviations disabled, skip mode refuses prefixes of declared long names
such as `--prof` or `--prof=value` for `--profile`. unrelated undeclared options
are still skipped.

skip mode also refuses short-option tokens containing a declared option behind
an undeclared letter. for example, a requirement on `-x` refuses `-kxpost` when
`-k` is undeclared, since skipping it could hide an override of `-x`. declare
`-k` as a flag to parse that cluster normally. a declared valued option still
consumes its attached suffix as a value.

for a worked example of forwarding `--watch` to a project script, see
[argument matching](policy-rules.md#match-text-and-arguments). use requirements
with an `on_unmet` branch when an option violation should contribute a rejection
instead of making the entire rule miss.

## locations and domains

an `argv` rule can match the executable, arguments, and cwd. file rules match
typed file operations. shell rules match shell input. web rules match searches,
fetches and supported loopback http requests. mcp rules match mcp requests.
`exact_request` binds the complete
normalized input and context rather than just the command arguments. the guided
cli defaults to that exact-request form; explicitly choosing `argv` broadens the
vendor/environment binding.

path predicates use `exact`, `within`, or `outside`. references use `project`,
`absolute`, `read`, or `write` roots. read/write roots require
`access-paths-v1`; their configured directories are described in
[additional access paths](project-review.md#additional-access-paths).

use a cwd predicate to constrain where a command starts. use target predicates
to constrain its observed file effects. use `argument_paths` to check explicit
path operands without claiming a complete model of the tool's effects.
see [path restrictions and supported operations](policy-rules.md#restrict-paths)
and [web rules](policy-rules.md#allow-searches-and-documentation-fetches).

mcp rules can check explicit path arguments with `field_paths`, for example
`field_paths: {/project: {path: {within: {root: write}}, absolute: true}}`.
this requires `field-paths-v1`, `location-v1` and `access-paths-v1`. paths use
filesystem observations, including symlink resolution; unavailable evidence
does not establish permission. `absolute: true` requires an absolute path.
without `relative_to`, relative paths fail the predicate. use absolute paths
when the server's path base is unknown, `relative_to: cwd` only when it shares
the request context's working folder, or
`relative_to: project` when a verified launcher starts the server at the
enrolled project root.

to check paths inside an array, point the `field_paths` key at the array and set
`each` to the json pointer for a path within each item, such as `/path`. an empty
`each` checks each item directly. missing path members are skipped. a malformed
array, a present non-string path, or more than 128 array items across one
predicate fails the check. this also requires `field-path-arrays-v1`.

### local http requests

use action `request` to review a shell http operation by method and endpoint.
declare `local-http-requests-v1` and specify both `method` and `url`. the
following rule permits a post to one development endpoint on the loopback
interface.

```yaml
id: reload-local-service
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: web
  action: request
  method: post
  url:
    schemes: [http]
    hosts: [127.0.0.1]
    ports: [8080]
    path: {exact: /-/reload}
  request_fields:
    /body: {exact: false}
```

the command can use `curl --request post http://127.0.0.1:8080/-/reload`.
curl can also pin a `localhost` or `.localhost` hostname to loopback.
put `-q` first, pass `--noproxy '*'`, and use a matching pin such as
`--resolve api.localhost:8080:127.0.0.1`. the rule matches the url's
hostname and port. wget uses the literal `127.0.0.1` address.
use literal paths with percent escapes and dot segments omitted.

for an endpoint you trust through ordinary hostname resolution, declare
`local-http-hostname-resolution-v1` and add `/hostname_resolution: {exact: system}`.
this requires one scheme, one exact `localhost` or `.localhost` hostname, one
port and one exact path in `conditions.url`. it covers host curl commands
without a `--resolve` pin. shield checks command options, client configuration
and proxy settings. use a pinned request when the connection must stay on ipv4
loopback regardless of hostname resolution.

for example, allow one reviewed read-only mcp tool on a workspace endpoint:

```yaml
id: query-workspace-metrics
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: web
  action: request
  method: post
  url:
    schemes: [http]
    hosts: [metrics.workspace.localhost]
    ports: [8080]
    path: {exact: /mcp}
  request_fields:
    /hostname_resolution: {exact: system}
    /rpc_method: {exact: tools/call}
    /rpc_tool: {exact: query_metrics}
```

put related endpoint rules into one `policy_propose` review. select handshake
operations by `/rpc_method`, and tool calls by both `/rpc_method` and `/rpc_tool`.
review the effect of each tool at the endpoint before allowing it.

`request_fields` uses json pointer selectors. `/client` is `shell` and
`/redirects` is `none`. `/body` and `/basic_auth` are booleans.
`/headers` is an array of lowercased header names. for a recognized json-rpc
body, `/rpc_method` contains the method and `/rpc_tool` contains the tool
name for `tools/call`. header values and credentials are absent from these
fields. a fetch rule covers its own separate action.

### isolated docker validators

the `docker_isolated_bind` requirement checks a `docker --context name run`
invocation. declare `docker-isolated-bind-v1`, `argument-rules-v1`,
`requirements-v1` and `location-v1` alongside `structured-rules-v1`.

```yaml
id: validate-local-config
decision: allow
conditions:
  domain: argv
  executable: docker
  arguments:
    kind: options
    prefix: [--context, dev, run]
    flags: [--rm]
    values: [--pull, --network, --mount, --env]
    require_all: [--rm, --pull, --network, --mount]
    parse: stop_at_operand
    operands:
      match: {one_of: ["acme/validator:1", check, /etc/acme/config.yml]}
      min: 3
      max: 3
  cwd: {exact: {root: project}}
requirements:
  docker_isolated_bind:
    context: dev
    image: "acme/validator:1"
    command: [check, /etc/acme/config.yml]
    source: {exact: {root: project, path: config.yml}}
    target: /etc/acme/config.yml
    environment: [mode=validate]
on_unmet:
  decision: ask
```

`context` selects the operator's docker context. `image` and `command`
match the literal image reference and its entrypoint arguments. use a digest
if the image identity must be immutable. `source` selects an existing
regular project file and `target` names its absolute container path.
the optional `environment` lists permitted literal `name=value`
assignments for `--env`.

the run requires `--rm`, `--pull never`, `--network none` and a single
`--mount type=bind,source=…,target=…,readonly`. the source check covers the
cli host file. shield still asks about the image entrypoint because the
docker daemon resolves the mounted file on its own host.
for the rule above, the command is:

```sh
docker --context dev run --rm --pull never --network none \
  --mount type=bind,source=./config.yml,target=/etc/acme/config.yml,readonly \
  --env mode=validate acme/validator:1 check /etc/acme/config.yml
```

## graphql requests

an argv predicate `graphql: {carrier: gh-api, operation: query}` verifies a
supported inline `gh api graphql` query. it requires `graphql-v1` and the ordinary
argument/executable selectors. parsing does not itself allow the request: the
rule's decision, requirements, other policy and host restrictions still apply.
custom rules and packs can declare this implemented capability and supply their
own reviewed selection models. engine support does not add query permissions to
installed packs; inspect their actual rules before relying on an allowance.

the carrier accepts inline `-f` strings and scalar `-f` fields, one selected
query operation, scalar defaults, aliases and fragments. optional `operationname`
selects a named operation. `--paginate` requires a nullable `$endcursor: string`
used only in cursor arguments. supported output flags are `--silent`,
`--include`/`-i` and paginated `--slurp`; explicit method/hostname are limited to
`post` and `github.com`. known conflicting host context fails verification.

file/stdin input, typed placeholders, object-valued variables, list values, mutations,
custom headers, alternate endpoints/hosts, `--jq`, templates and unknown syntax
do not satisfy a query predicate; [mutation predicates](#graphql-mutations)
admit reviewed mutations and their input objects. a query classification
without `selection` accepts structurally valid object argument literals and asserts
no repository scope. source names and related metadata checks do not attest the
actual network destination or immutable repository identity.

an optional `selection` has `root` and `states`. each state declares accepted
fragment `types` and a `fields` map. a field has either `leaf: true` or
`select: state`, plus optional `arguments`. query-root fields can instead use
`subtree: true` with `graphql-subtree-v1`: their own arguments are checked, but
all descendant fields, arguments and fragment types are unrestricted. a subtree
requires a child selection and can appear only in the root state with exactly
`types: [query]`. it permits related objects outside the named repository.
document, variable, directive and resource checks still apply; descendant object
argument literals are accepted within the existing input-depth bounds, while
list inputs and object-valued variables remain unsupported.
each argument declares `match` as
`{text: selector}`, `{exact: scalar}` or `{scalar: string|integer|number|boolean|enum}`,
with optional `required`, `nullable` and `cursor` booleans defaulting to false.
every modeled field and argument must be declared; aliases do not replace actual
field names. missing required scope values and unknown modeled traversals fail. a cursor
declaration must be optional, nullable and `{scalar: string}`. pack text selectors
can use prepared variable projections. source models contain no executable code
or live schema queries. invalid models make the policy files invalid; exhausted analysis
limits block rather than falling back to an allowance.
rules using this predicate cannot export `agents.codex.prefixes`: a command
prefix cannot represent query or selection constraints.

for example, this requirement fragment admits name metadata only from the named
repository; put it inside an argv rule's `requirements` and supply `on_unmet`:

```yaml
graphql:
  carrier: gh-api
  operation: query
  selection:
    root: query
    states:
      query:
        types: [query]
        fields:
          repository:
            arguments:
              owner: {required: true, match: {text: acme}}
              name: {required: true, match: {text: web}}
            select: repository
      repository:
        types: [repository]
        fields:
          namewithowner: {leaf: true}
```

the query `{ repository(owner:"acme", name:"web") { namewithowner } }` satisfies
this model; adding `parent { namewithowner }` does not. use a deny unmet branch
when failure must block rather than follow ask fallback. see
[conditions and requirements](policy-rules.md#conditions-versus-requirements).

for a root-only boundary, replace `select: repository` with `subtree: true`
and omit the `repository` state. every root must still be declared and match
its arguments, including roots inside fragments and conditional selections.
nested reads such as `parent { namewithowner }` then pass without a field inventory.

### graphql mutations

`graphql: {carrier: gh-api, operation: mutation, root_fields: [...], selection: ...}`
classifies a selected mutation by the root fields it calls. it requires
`graphql-mutations-v1` in addition to `graphql-v1`. it checks the request's
shape, not its target: github mutations name objects by opaque ids, which shield
does not look up, so a mutation predicate never confirms which repository it
changes.

- `selection` is required, and its root state's `types` must be exactly
  `[mutation]`. list every mutation you review in that one model, with its
  arguments and the payload fields it may return. a request calling any other
  root field fails the predicate.
- `root_fields` names one class of those mutations. the predicate is met when
  the request calls at least one of them. give each class its own rule with the
  same model: a request calling fields from several classes meets each of their
  rules, and the strictest decision applies. fields under fragments or
  `@skip`/`@include` count; aliases do not replace actual names.
- an input object argument uses `match: {object: {field: argument}}`, whose
  fields follow the argument rules above and may nest up to four levels. every
  input field must be declared, and a repeated key fails. object matchers are
  accepted only in mutation models. lists, object-typed variables and
  `--paginate` do not satisfy a mutation predicate.

for example, this condition matches requests that resolve or unresolve review
threads and return only the thread's id and state:

```yaml
graphql:
  carrier: gh-api
  operation: mutation
  root_fields: [resolvereviewthread, unresolvereviewthread]
  selection:
    root: mutation
    states:
      mutation:
        types: [mutation]
        fields:
          resolvereviewthread:
            arguments:
              input:
                required: true
                match:
                  object:
                    threadid: {required: true, match: {scalar: string}}
            select: payload
          unresolvereviewthread:
            arguments:
              input:
                required: true
                match:
                  object:
                    threadid: {required: true, match: {scalar: string}}
            select: payload
      payload:
        types: [resolvereviewthreadpayload, unresolvereviewthreadpayload]
        fields:
          thread: {select: thread}
      thread:
        types: [pullrequestreviewthread]
        fields:
          id: {leaf: true}
          isresolved: {leaf: true}
```

`mutation { resolvereviewthread(input:{threadid:"t1"}) { thread { id isresolved } } }`
meets it; adding `pullrequest { title }` under `thread` does not.

## capabilities

typed json field maps (`fields`, `request_fields` and mcp `connection`) accept
`{not: {exact: value}}` to match a present value unequal to `value`. missing
fields never match this predicate; a present null remains distinct from absence.
for example, `/env: {not: {exact: {}}}` detects supplied non-empty environment
maps without matching an omitted or empty map. this requires both
`field-negation-v1` and `negated-selectors-v1`. nested field negation and negated
text predicates are not accepted; use a text selector's own `not` for the latter.

## agent workflow

before a known batch of privileged commands, inspect `session_grant_show`.
shield's native hook supplies a `session_ref` after an ordinary shell request;
this reference selects a recorded conversation, and grants no permission.

call `session_grant_propose` with that reference, an `idempotency_key`, and a
`scope` array. every array entry is an alternative; all constraints within an
entry must match. entries use the normal argv rule `conditions` and optional
`requirements`. supported entries require literal executable names, a project
cwd constraint, and exact arguments or a closed options grammar. unknown
options, opaque shell requests, and non-shell tools cannot use a grant.
requests whose policy analysis remaps argv to another directory or a file
consumer also retain their ordinary approval route.

this example permits two exact commands from the project root:

```json
{
  "session_ref": "copy_the_native_session_ref",
  "idempotency_key": "dependency-merges-1",
  "duration_seconds": 7200,
  "reason": "merge the two dependency prs after completing their reviews.",
  "scope": [
    {
      "conditions": {
        "domain": "argv",
        "executable": "gh",
        "arguments": {
          "kind": "exact",
          "values": ["pr", "merge", "42", "--repo", "acme/app", "--squash"]
        },
        "cwd": {"exact": {"root": "project"}}
      }
    },
    {
      "conditions": {
        "domain": "argv",
        "executable": "gh",
        "arguments": {
          "kind": "exact",
          "values": ["pr", "merge", "43", "--repo", "acme/app", "--squash"]
        },
        "cwd": {"exact": {"root": "project"}}
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

copy the returned `apply_arguments` unchanged to `session_grant_approve`. shield
shows its confirmation form to the person. accepting a tool-call permission,
a chat message, or an automatic command review does not accept this form.
if forms are unavailable, the person can review the candidate in their terminal.
the agent must not run the operator approval command itself.

after acceptance, submit covered native commands normally. no grant id is added
to commands. shield checks the recorded host conversation, current policy and
protection state, expiry, every covered operation, and the scope on each use.
it records the original policy decision separately from grant authorization.

for exact git alternatives with an exact project cwd, preparation returns
`scope_checks` and includes the findings in the approval form. each finding
names its alternative and reports `clear_at_preparation`,
`one_time_approval_required`, `protected_access_refused` or `context_unavailable`.
a grant cannot override a failed protected-file check. use the native
`request_approve` route when one-time approval is available. these findings
describe preparation time; every native use checks again. argument families
and varying cwd scopes are checked at use time.

git checks use the worktree root reported by git, including when commands run
through a separate repository entry directory. `stash apply` and `stash pop`
can follow ordinary policy when inspection finds no protected-file changes in
the saved worktree, index or untracked-file trees. changed protected files,
unavailable stash objects and unsupported arguments retain separate review.
numeric stash references require one-time review because git interprets them as
stash indexes. use an explicit `refs/stash@{n}` reference for inspection; the
omitted-reference default is `refs/stash@{0}`.

repeat proposals and accepted apply calls reuse the retained result; they do
not extend its expiry. equivalent pending, active or declined offers return the
existing record. do not repeatedly offer declined permission or broaden the
scope to work around a refusal.

an offer waits for the person's answer however long they take. it is withdrawn
when its agent session ends (the host's `sessionend` hook; the end of a turn
leaves it open) or when the project already holds 64 open offers and a new one
needs room: the requesting conversation's oldest open offer goes first, then the
oldest of any conversation. a withdrawn offer cannot be approved; propose again
to get a fresh review.

## reconsider a declined offer

if the person explicitly asks to reconsider, inspect the declined record with
`session_grant_show`. call `session_grant_reconsider` using its `proposal_id`,
`candidate_digest` and a fresh `idempotency_key`:

```json
{
  "proposal_id": "copy_the_declined_proposal_id",
  "candidate_digest": "copy_its_candidate_digest",
  "idempotency_key": "explicit-reconsideration-1"
}
```

this prepares a new candidate with the same recorded conversation, scope,
duration, reason and deny overrides. it preserves the original decline and grants
no permission. copy the new candidate's `apply_arguments` to
`session_grant_approve`. the fresh form identifies the earlier decline and shows
the complete permission again. accept issues the new grant; decline or cancel
leaves both decisions recorded without permission.

do not call reconsideration automatically. changing a normal proposal's retry
key alone keeps the decline suppressed. repeating the same reconsideration key
returns its retained result; another key cannot duplicate a matching pending
review or renew a live grant. a fresh decline stays suppressed too. changed
policy, protection, registration or an unavailable native context requires
inspection and a current proposal, rather than reviving the old candidate.

## what the person approves

the review identifies the project, agent and recorded conversation, the complete
scope, lifetime, and any explicitly named deny overrides. shared mcp servers may
have no trusted link to the current conversation; the form states this and
explicitly targets the recorded conversation shown.

the default lifetime is two hours, with a minimum of one minute and maximum of
eight hours. matching uses are unlimited during that period. resuming the same
conversation can reuse an unexpired grant. a new conversation cannot. process
exit is not evidence that a conversation ended.

revocation, changed protection settings, and changed native
registration invalidate the permission. clock discontinuities also make it
unavailable; obtain fresh confirmation. a system restart or suspend may trigger
this conservative clock check on some platforms.

an ordinary grant covers ask decisions. to override a policy deny, the agent
must select each current rule through `rule_list` and include its `rule_ref`,
`branch: "met"`, and `rule_digest` in `override_denies`. shield prominently shows
these exceptions. failed requirements, preconditions, fixed protected state and
unresolved operations cannot be overridden this way.

permission does not prove that review happened, remote checks passed, or a
command succeeded. continue checking those task requirements before execution.

## inspect and revoke

```sh
shield session-grant list
shield session-grant show proposal_or_grant_id
shield session-grant propose candidate.json
shield session-grant approve proposal_id
shield session-grant revoke proposal_or_grant_id
shield history list --authorization-kind session_grant
shield history list --grant-id grant_id
```

approval and operator revocation require the controlling terminal. json mode is
read-only. agents inspect through `session_grant_show` and can reduce their own
authority through `session_grant_revoke`; another connection's grant may require
operator revocation. history is optional and does not own live permission.

list inspection accepts `session_ref`, `cursor` and `limit` (1–64, default 16).
selecting a `proposal_id` or `grant_id` returns one record and cannot be combined
with paging. restart pagination when state changes and its cursor becomes stale.
terminal receipts remain available for up to 24 hours before reclamation.

existing installations retain saved mcp tool permissions. after installing a
build with these tools, rerun `shield mcp setup` for the selected agent, review
its tool permissions, and restart the agent so it loads the new catalog.
